Topic: llm-architecture

What is inside a large language model and why it is built that way, derived from first principles: the decoder block, attention and its variants, the feed-forward and mixture of experts, position, normalisation and the residual stream, long context, state-space and hybrid models, and the families and training objectives. Tiny models trained on an Apple M1 Pro, a small open model inspected, frontier models compared from their configs, published results kept apart. Data as of October 2026.
0 One screen1 What it computes2 One block3 Attention and its cache4 Attention variants5 Position6 FFN and MoE7 Norms and stability8 The arithmetic9 Long context10 Beyond attention11 Families12 Read a config13 ChoosingMistakesInterviewChild pages

A large language model (LLM) is a function that reads a sequence of tokens and returns, for the next position, a probability for every token in its vocabulary. Almost every LLM in use in 2026 computes that function with the same machine: a stack of identical decoder blocks, each mixing information across positions (attention, or a recurrent substitute) and then transforming each position on its own (a feed-forward network), with a normalisation and a residual connection around each. This page follows one token through one block, then asks at each component what the alternatives are and what each one costs, in parameters, in FLOPs and in the memory a running model must hold. Reading time about 39 minutes (measured from the words outside widgets at 200 a minute; the folded answers add about 7).

The page serves four goals: write and modify a GPT block, know what every tensor in it is and costs, debug a model that misbehaves, and answer design questions in an interview. Neighbouring pages own their subjects and are linked, not repeated: Topic: llm-landscape (labs, models, prices), Topic: llm-training-and-post-training (how these models are trained), Batching, KV cache and scheduling (how they are served), and Performance math (the hardware side of FLOPs and bytes).

1. What an LLM computes: tokens in, a distribution out

Text is first cut into tokens, integer ids from a fixed vocabulary of size V, by a tokenizer (Llama 3.1 uses V = 128,256, config). The model then runs a fixed pipeline on each position:

Embedrow id of a V × d table: one vector of d numbers per token
→
L blockseach adds attention, then a feed-forward, to that vector
→
Final normrescale the vector
→
Unembedd × V matrix: one score (logit) per vocabulary entry
→
Softmaxlogits become probabilities that sum to 1

The vector of d numbers a position carries through the stack is the residual stream: every block reads it and adds its output back, so it is the model's working memory for that position. The scores before the softmax are the logits. In training, every position predicts its own next token at once and the loss is the average cross-entropy (minus the log probability given to the true next token); a causal mask stops a position from looking at later ones, so one forward pass over a 4,096-token sequence gives 4,096 training examples. In generation, the model predicts one token, appends it, and runs again (how the next token is picked from the distribution is Sampling and decoding).

Two small choices live here. The embedding and unembedding matrices both have V × d entries; tied embeddings use one matrix for both (Press and Wolf 2016), which small models do because the table is a large share of their parameters (Llama 3.1 8B does not tie, "tie_word_embeddings": false; its two tables are 1.05 billion of its 8.03 billion parameters, derived as 2 × 128,256 × 4,096). And the vocabulary size trades sequence length against table size: a bigger vocabulary needs fewer tokens per sentence, so attention is cheaper, but each token is rarer in training. How tokenizers are trained and fail is Tokenizers.

Go deeper (optional): Tokenizers (BPE, byte-level, unigram, the language tax, glitch tokens); the logit lens in the Inside a real model lab shows what the residual stream would predict if the model stopped after each layer.

2. One token through one block

A block does two things to the residual stream x of every position, each wrapped the same way: normalise a copy, transform it, add the result back. In the pre-norm layout every current model uses (section 7):

h = x + Attention(Norm(x))
x′ = h + FFN(Norm(h))
x, h, x′
the residual stream before, between and after the two sublayers: one vector of d numbers per position
Attention
the only step where a position reads other positions (section 3)
FFN
the feed-forward network: the same small MLP applied to each position on its own (section 6)

Because each sublayer only adds to x, information written by layer 3 is still there, unchanged, for layer 30 to read, and gradients flow back along the same identity path. That is why a stack of 80 or 126 such blocks trains at all. The table follows one token through one block of Llama 3.1 8B, read from its config, with the matrix sizes that set its parameters and FLOPs:

RoPERotate Q and K by the position (section 5)samenone

derived from the Llama 3.1 8B config (hidden_size 4,096, 32 heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, intermediate_size 14,336, no biases): 218.1M weights per block, 41.9M in attention and 176.2M (81%) in the FFN. The tiny GPT of the running example: TODO 3 (setup): the same column for the tiny GPT (d_model, heads, FFN width, parameters per block). The code that does each step, with file and line at a pinned transformers version, is in the Block lab.

Predict: in one Llama 3.1 8B block, what share of the weights sits in the feed-forward network rather than in attention?
derived 176.2M of 218.1M, 81%. The classic block (full multi-head attention, FFN width 4d) has 4d² in attention and 8d² in the FFN, two thirds; GQA shrinks K and V by 4 times and the FFN here is 3.5d wide with three matrices, which pushes the FFN share up. That is why mixture of experts (section 6) targets the FFN: it is where the parameters are.

Each weight is used once per token in one multiply and one add, so a forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per weight per token; the backward pass costs about twice the forward, giving the 6N FLOPs per training token rule (Kaplan et al. 2020, section 2.1). Attention adds a term that grows with how many tokens are attended to (section 8).

3. Attention, and why it needs a cache

The problem. A token's meaning depends on earlier tokens ("it" needs its referent). Attention lets each position build its output as a weighted average of earlier positions' information, with weights the model computes from the content. Each position makes three vectors from its normalised residual stream: a query (what it is looking for), a key (what it offers to be found by) and a value (what it passes on if chosen). For one head:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q K⊤ / √dh + M ) V
Q, K, V
T × dh matrices: one query, key and value row per position; dh is the head dimension (64 to 256 in current models)
Q K⊤
T × T scores: every query dotted with every key
√dh
a dot product of dh random terms has spread about √dh; dividing keeps the softmax from saturating into a one-hot as dh grows (Vaswani et al. 2017, section 3.2.1)
M
the causal mask: 0 where a query may look (itself and earlier), minus infinity for later positions

A layer runs H heads in parallel, each with its own projections, so different heads can track different relations (the previous token, a matching earlier token, the subject of the sentence; the Inside a real model lab finds such heads in a trained model). Their outputs are concatenated and projected back to d.

Why a cache. In generation, the new token's query must be scored against the keys of every earlier token, and those keys and values do not change when a token is appended (the mask stops earlier positions from seeing later ones). So they are computed once and stored: the KV cache. Generation then splits into two phases. Prefill runs the whole prompt at once, a large matrix multiply, limited by arithmetic. Decode produces one token per step, and each step must read every weight and the whole cache from memory to do little arithmetic, so it is limited by memory bandwidth. The cache costs:

KV bytes per token = 2 × L × Hkv × dh × b
2
keys and values
L
layers that keep a cache
Hkv
key-value heads per layer (the attention variant decides this, section 4)
b
bytes per number: 2 in BF16, 1 in FP8
Predict: Llama 3.1 70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads of 128) serving one request at its full 128K context (131,072 tokens), cache in BF16. How big is that request's KV cache?
derived 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes (320 KiB) per token, × 131,072 = 40 GiB, for one request. The weights are about 141 GB in BF16 (70.6 billion parameters × 2 bytes), so 4 such requests hold more cache than weights, and 32 would need 1.25 TiB. With full multi-head attention (64 KV heads) every number would be 8 times larger. At long context the attention design, not the parameter count, decides what a GPU can serve. (config)

When it matters and how to check. Short prompts and small batches: the weights dominate memory and the cache barely matters. Long contexts, many concurrent requests or agents with long histories: the cache dominates. To check a running server, look at its reported KV-cache capacity in tokens (vLLM prints it at start-up); to check a design, compute the formula above. FlashAttention changes how attention is computed (tiled, never storing the T × T matrix), not how much is cached (FlashAttention).

4. The attention variants, compared on one shape

Every variant answers one question differently: what must each token keep, per layer, for later tokens to read? The table holds the shape fixed at Llama 3.1 8B's (32 layers, 32 query heads of 128, BF16) and changes only the variant, so the cache column compares like with like.

Model attributions from their configs and papers: MQA, Shazeer 2019, GQA, Ainslie et al. 2023, DeepSeek-V2, Mistral 7B, Gemma 3 report, gpt-oss config, NSA.

Published evidence on the quality cost. The GQA paper converts existing multi-head checkpoints by continued training on "5% of original pre-training compute" and reports that "uptrained GQA achieves quality close to multi-head attention with comparable speed to MQA" (Ainslie et al. 2023, authors' own runs). DeepSeek reports that MLA in DeepSeek-V2 "reduces the KV cache by 93.3% and boosts the maximum generation throughput to 5.76 times", compared with its earlier dense DeepSeek 67B (DeepSeek-V2 abstract, vendor; that comparison also changes the model, so it is not MLA alone). Measured here on the tiny GPT with the same seed and token budget: TODO 4 (Attention lab): held-out loss and KV bytes per token for the mha, gqa2, mqa, mla and sliding-window presets, and the decode-step time against context on MPS.

MLA is the one variant that cuts the cache below aggressive GQA while DeepSeek reports quality at or above MHA; how it works (compress, decouple the position key, absorb the up-projections at decode) is animated step by step on DeepSeek, against the MHA it replaced. Sliding windows do not shrink what a token keeps, only how long it is kept: Gemma 3 27B keeps 496 KiB per token by the formula (62 layers, 16 KV heads of 128), but at 128K its 52 windowed layers (window 1,024) hold only 416 MiB together and its 10 global layers 10 GiB, about 10.4 GiB against the 62 GiB the per-token figure suggests (derived).

2026 configs push the same levers further (derived from each config.json as the Architecture map computes it: BF16, every cache-growing layer counted; sizes are the makers' cards, vendor). Gemma 4 31B keeps Gemma 3's 5 sliding layers (window 1,024) per global layer, and its 10 global layers store one tensor for both K and V (4 KV heads of 512): a 128K request holds about 5.8 GiB, against 105 GiB if every layer kept every token. GLM-5 moves from GQA to MLA with DeepSeek's sparse indexer, 87.75 KiB per token. DeepSeek-V3.2's main cache is DeepSeek-V3's 68.6 KiB per token, and its indexer keeps a second, smaller cache of keys, 15.25 KiB per token: 83.88 KiB with both (the Attention lab counts both; the map counts the main cache only). DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T parameters) goes further: each layer caches a history compressed 4 or 128 times plus a 128-token window, which neither tab computes; its design is on DeepSeek. The hybrids of section 10 keep attention in a few layers only: Kimi K3 (2.8T total, 104B active) has MLA in 24 of its 93 layers, 27 KiB per token, and Nemotron 3 Super (120B, 12B active) 8 attention layers with 2 KV heads beside 40 Mamba-2 layers, 8 KiB per token.

Attention sinks. Trained models put a large share of attention on the first token whatever it is, a place to "park" attention when nothing else is relevant. Drop the first tokens from a sliding cache and quality collapses; keep a few of them and window attention works on streams of "up to 4 million tokens" (StreamingLLM, Xiao et al. 2023). Measured on SmolLM2: TODO 5 (Inside lab): share of attention on the first token by layer, and what happens when it is removed.

5. Position: telling attention where each token sits

The problem. Attention by itself is blind to order: shuffle the earlier tokens and each query gets the same weighted average. Something must inject position. The answers in order of arrival:

  • Absolute, added to the embedding. Fixed sinusoids (Vaswani et al. 2017) or a learned vector per position (GPT-2, 1,024 positions). A learned table has nothing for position 1,025.
  • RoPE (rotary position embedding) (Su et al., RoFormer): split each query and key into pairs of numbers and rotate pair i by the angle position × θi, with θi = base−2i/dh. Rotations compose, so the query-key dot product depends only on the distance between the two tokens. No parameters; the near-universal default. The base sets the slowest rotation: 10,000 in the original, 500,000 in Llama 3.1 (rope_theta), larger for longer context.
  • ALiBi: no rotation, a penalty on each score proportional to distance (Press et al. 2021), built to extrapolate.
  • NoPE: no position signal at all; a causal decoder can still infer order from the mask. Used on some layers of recent models (one in four in SmolLM3, config).

Past the trained length. A model trained on 8K tokens has never seen the rotation angles of position 100,000 in its slow pairs, and quality collapses there. The fixes stretch the angles back into the trained range: position interpolation (Chen et al. 2023), base scaling, and YaRN, which stretches only the slow pairs (Peng et al. 2023), each followed by a short training phase at the longer length. The rule ships in the config: Llama 3.1 has "rope_scaling": {"rope_type": "llama3", "factor": 8.0, "original_max_position_embeddings": 8192}; gpt-oss uses YaRN with factor 32 from 4,096 to 131,072 (config). Drop that field when copying a config and the model still loads, still answers short prompts well, and degrades past the original length.

Go deeper (optional): Positional Encodings owns the schemes, the extension methods and their configs, and its Past the trained length tab runs five schemes trained here past their 256 tokens; Long context what breaks past the trained length.

6. The feed-forward network, and mixture of experts

What the FFN does. After attention has gathered information from other positions, the FFN transforms each position on its own: expand to a wider hidden layer, apply a nonlinearity, project back. It holds most of the parameters (81% of a Llama 3.1 8B block, section 2) and behaves like a key-value memory where many stored facts are found (Geva et al. 2021). The original used ReLU at width 4d (2,048 for d = 512, Vaswani et al. 2017); current models use SwiGLU, a gated variant with three matrices instead of two: out = Wdown( SiLU(Wgatex) × Wupx ). It improved quality at equal compute in Shazeer 2020, which shrank the width to 2/3 of 4d (8d/3) so the three matrices cost what two did; Llama 3.1 8B uses 14,336 = 3.5d.

Mixture of experts (MoE). Replace the one FFN by E smaller FFNs (experts) and a router, a linear layer that scores every expert for each token; the token goes to its top k experts and their outputs are summed, weighted by the router scores. The model then has many parameters (memory, knowledge) but each token pays for only k experts (compute, latency). Two numbers describe it: total parameters (what must sit in memory) and active parameters (what one token uses). DeepSeek-V3 has 256 routed experts plus 1 shared expert that every token uses, 8 routed per token: in one of its MoE layers the experts hold 11.3 billion weights and a token uses 0.40 billion of them, 3.5% (derived from its config: experts of 3 × 7,168 × 2,048); the whole model is 671B total and 37B active (DeepSeek-V3 report, vendor).

The same batch of 8 tokens through a dense FFN and through an MoE layer (8 experts, top 2)

Router probabilities measured: block 2 of the tiny GPT's moe8top2 run (8 experts, top 2, softmax router with the auxiliary balancing loss) on the first 8 tokens of the running sequence, recorded by the Mixture of experts child (router_probs_8tok.json). Scale is drawn the Mixtral way, one expert box per FFN of the dense model's size; in the tiny GPT each expert is half the dense FFN, so its 2 active experts cost what the dense FFN costs. That run trained without a capacity limit; the capacity factor 1.25 here is applied to its recorded choices: 1.25 × 8 × 2 / 8 = 2.5, rounded up to 3 tokens per expert (the tiny GPT's code uses math.ceil; implementations that round down would allow 2), and assignments over the limit are dropped and pass through on the residual stream only.

What it costs and what goes wrong. Experts must stay busy in equal measure: a router that sends most tokens to a few experts wastes the rest and, with a fixed capacity per expert, drops the overflow (the token skips the FFN). The classic fix is an auxiliary loss that rewards balanced routing (Switch Transformers); DeepSeek-V3 instead adds a per-expert bias to the routing scores, nudged after each step, and reports this "auxiliary-loss-free" scheme beats the loss (DeepSeek-V3 report, vendor). The trend is from few large experts (Mixtral 8x7B: 8 experts, top 2, Mixtral) to many small ones (Qwen3-235B-A22B: 128 experts, top 8, no shared expert, Qwen3 report). Serving an MoE needs memory for every expert and enough tokens per batch that each expert gets a useful share; spread over GPUs it needs expert parallelism and its all-to-all traffic.

Measured on the tiny GPT (Mixture of experts child; 1,500 steps of 8,192 tokens, equal active FFN, held-out loss): dense 2.278, 8 experts top 2 2.256, 16 fine-grained experts top 3 plus 1 shared expert 2.210. The 8-expert gain (0.022) is about the size of the seed-to-seed spread (dense 2.264 and MoE 2.254 with seed 1), so only the fine-grained, shared-expert layout clearly beats dense here. Without any balancing the router collapses as described: in the worst layer one expert takes 48% of assignments and 14 of the 48 experts get under 1% (loss 2.296).

7. Normalisation, residuals and stability

The problem. Deep stacks are hard to train: activations and gradients grow or shrink layer by layer. A normalisation layer rescales a vector to a standard size. The 2017 Transformer put it after the residual add, post-norm: x′ = Norm(x + F(x)). That normalises the residual stream itself, and deep post-norm models need a careful learning-rate warmup to train at all. Pre-norm, x′ = x + F(Norm(x)), normalises only the copy each sublayer reads and leaves an untouched identity path through the stack; Xiong et al. 2020 argued from the gradients at initialisation that pre-norm can drop the warmup (their claim; not measured here, every run on this page uses a 100-step warmup). Its known cost is that the stream's size grows with depth, since every layer only adds. Measured on the tiny GPT with the same seed and budget: TODO 7 (Block lab): residual-stream norm by layer under pre- and post-norm, and the learning rate at which post-norm diverges (loss and gradient-norm numbers).

Measured on the tiny GPT (Normalisation, residuals and stability child, 1,500 steps, held-out loss): at a learning rate ten times the default (3e-2) without clipping, the largest attention logit climbs to 20,865 and the run ends at 4.295. QK-norm alone brings it to 2.432 (largest logit 69.9); a z-loss on the output logits does not stop the attention logits (4.289); capping attention logits at 50 helps partly (2.845); gradient clipping at 1.0 is no fix (4.361, the Block lab's run). The two other placements need QK-norm to work: the norm after each sublayer (OLMo 2's) goes from 3.405 to 2.506 with it, the sandwich (Gemma's) from 2.501 to 2.396, at the default rate.

  • RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich 2019) divides by the root mean square and drops LayerNorm's mean subtraction and bias: one reduction instead of two, no measured quality loss; universal in current models.
  • QK-norm: RMSNorm on queries and keys before the dot product, so attention scores cannot grow without bound during training, a known source of loss spikes (Dehghani et al. 2023; used in OLMo 2, Gemma 3 and Qwen3).
  • Norms after the sublayer: OLMo 2 normalises each sublayer's output before adding it, x + Norm(F(x)), still with a clean residual path; Gemma 3 normalises both before and after (Gemma 3 report).
  • Newer variants, read from configs and code (transformers v5.20.1): Gemma 4 multiplies by a plain RMSNorm gain where Gemma 1 to 3 used 1 + gain (modeling_gemma4.py line 222); MiniMax-M1 keeps post-norm with DeepNorm's residual scale, α = (2 × 80)1/4 ≈ 3.5566 for its 80 layers (layernorm_*_alpha in its config); DeepSeek-V4 widens the residual stream into 4 streams mixed by a doubly stochastic matrix, manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC, arXiv 2512.24880), with pre-norm RMSNorm inside.

How to check a run. A loss spike is a sudden jump in training loss, sometimes recovered, sometimes not. Log the global gradient norm, the largest attention logit and the per-layer residual norms: a spike preceded by growing attention logits points at QK-norm or a lower learning rate; a single bad batch points at data. Large models also show a few massive activations, single residual-stream dimensions thousands of times larger than the rest (Sun et al. 2024), which matter for low-precision training and quantisation. Measured on SmolLM2: TODO 8 (Inside lab): largest residual dimension against the median, by layer.

8. Depth, width, and the arithmetic that ties it together

Three numbers answer most questions about a model, and all three come from its config in a minute: parameters, FLOPs per token, and KV bytes per token (section 3).

N ≈ L × (attention + FFN) + 2Vd
FLOPs per token ≈ 2N + 4 L T H dh
attention
2d² for Q and output, plus 2 d Hkv dh for K and V (4d² with full MHA)
FFN
3 d dff for SwiGLU (2 d dff for a plain MLP; 8d² at dff = 4d, hence the classic 12 L d²)
2Vd
embedding and unembedding (Vd once if tied)
4 L T H dh
the attention term of the forward pass for one token attending to T earlier tokens: scores Q K⊤ and the weighted sum with V, 2 FLOPs per multiply-add each

Worked: Llama 3.1 8B. 32 blocks of 218.1M (section 2) = 6.98B, plus two 525.3M embedding tables and a final norm = 8.03B parameters, the published size (derived, matches the 8.03B on its model page). Forward FLOPs per token: 2N = 15.0 GFLOP. The attention term at T = 131,072: 4 × 32 × 131,072 × 4,096 = 68.7 GFLOP, more than four times the weights' share. The two are equal at T ≈ 28,600 tokens: below that a token's cost is set by the parameter count, above it by the context (derived). Training costs about three times the forward, the 6N rule of section 2 (plus three times the attention term).

Depth against width. At a fixed parameter count, shape matters less than one might think: Kaplan et al. 2020 found that "other architectural details such as network width or depth have minimal effects within a wide range" (abstract). It matters for speed: each layer is a sequential step, so a deeper model of the same size has more latency per token and less to parallelise per step. Small models are the exception that go deep and thin: Meta's MobileLLM reports that at under a billion parameters depth beats width (Liu et al. 2024, vendor), and SmolLM2-135M is 30 layers of 576. Checked on every saved config: TODO 10 (Config calculator): parameter-count residuals against published sizes for every config in src/data/configs/, and the largest one explained.

9. Long context: four walls

A model "supports 128K tokens" only if it clears four separate limits, each with its own remedy:

  1. Memory: the KV cache grows linearly with context (40 GiB per 128K request for Llama 3.1 70B, section 3). Remedies: fewer KV heads (GQA, MQA), compressed caches (MLA), windowed layers, FP8 caches, layers without a cache (section 10).
  2. Compute: prefill attention grows with the square of the prompt length; past about 29K tokens it is most of Llama 3.1 8B's work (section 8). Remedies: sliding windows, trained sparse attention, linear layers.
  3. Position: rotation angles past the trained length were never seen (section 5). Remedy: RoPE scaling plus a long-context training phase.
  4. Use: a model can fit and run 128K tokens and still fail to use them. RULER found that of models claiming 32K or more, "only half of them can maintain satisfactory performance at the length of 32K" (Hsieh et al. 2024, third-party); information in the middle of a long prompt is used worse than at its ends (Liu et al. 2023). The claimed context is a ceiling, the effective context is measured.

Measured (on the Long context child, CPU): SmolLM2-135M, whose config allows 8,192 positions, finds a pass key 80% of the time at 8,192 tokens and never at 12,288 or 16,384 (wall 3). Wall 4 hides behind perplexity: at 4,096 tokens, evicting three quarters of its KV cache with scores computed before the question is seen drops retrieval from 97% to 0%, while H2O eviction down to 12.5% of the cache moves the loss on a new story only from 2.07 to 2.10. And a model trained with a window has no position wall: the tiny GPT with window 64 (RoPE, trained on 256 tokens) scores 2.09 on positions 1,024 to 2,047, where the same model with full attention scores 3.82.

How to check: compute the cache at the target context and concurrency (wall 1), time a prefill at that length (wall 2), read rope_scaling and max_position_embeddings (wall 3), and run a long-context benchmark at the length you need, not the length on the card (wall 4).

Go deeper (optional): Long context owns cache growth and compression, local and global layouts and effective context; Long-context and multimodal benchmarks owns how it is measured.

10. Beyond attention: state-space models, linear attention and hybrids

The problem. Attention keeps everything: memory grows with every token and each new token reads all of it. A recurrent layer keeps a fixed-size state instead and updates it once per token, so memory and work per token stay constant however long the context. Linear attention writes each token's value into a matrix state indexed by its key (St = St−1 + vtkt⊤, read out as Stqt); a state-space model (SSM) runs a linear recurrence ht = Atht−1 + Btxt, yt = Ctht. What made them competitive was making the update depend on the input, so the layer chooses what to keep and what to forget: Mamba's selective SSM (Mamba), and gated delta rules that erase what a key stored before writing (Gated DeltaNet, Yang et al. 2024). Training still runs in parallel over the sequence with a scan or chunked algorithm.

The same 8 tokens through one attention layer and one recurrent layer

Shapes from the Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B config: its attention layers keep 2 KV heads of 256 (1,024 numbers per token); its Gated DeltaNet layers keep 32 value heads with a 128 × 128 state (524,288 numbers, whatever the context). The chart is derived: one layer of each, numbers held against context; they cross at 512 tokens.

What it costs. A fixed state is a lossy summary: whatever was not written into it is gone. Jelassi et al. 2024 prove that "a two layer transformer can copy strings of exponential length while" fixed-state models "are fundamentally limited by their fixed-size latent state", and find pretrained transformers "dramatically outperform state space models at copying and retrieving information from context". Hence hybrids: mostly recurrent layers, with a few attention layers kept for exact recall. Jamba uses one attention layer per seven Mamba layers and reports a KV cache of about 4 GB at 256K tokens in 16-bit (Lieber et al. 2024, vendor); NVIDIA's Nemotron-H "replace[s] the majority of self-attention layers" with Mamba layers and reports "up to 3× faster" inference than comparable transformers (Nemotron-H, vendor); Qwen3-Next keeps full attention in every fourth layer (full_attention_interval: 4) and Gated DeltaNet in the rest, 24 KiB of cache per token against 96 KiB had all 48 layers been attention (derived).

By 2026 the hybrid is a flagship design (layer patterns and caches derived from the configs on the Architecture map; sizes from the model cards, vendor): Qwen3.5-397B-A17B keeps Qwen3-Next's 3 Gated DeltaNet layers per attention layer; NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Super (120B, 12B active) interleaves 40 Mamba-2 layers with 8 attention layers, 8 KiB of cache per token; Moonshot's Kimi K3 (2.8T, 104B active) puts 3 Kimi Delta Attention layers before each MLA layer, 27 KiB per token.

Measured on the tiny GPT (Beyond attention child; 1,500 steps of 8,192 tokens each, held-out loss on 100 windows / loss on the running sequence): an SSM-only model ties attention on held-out text, 2.152 against 2.160, but loses on the running sequence, whose repeated names reward exact recall, 2.024 against 1.741. Hybrids beat both: one attention layer in six 2.089 / 1.688, two in six 2.082 / 1.629. The copying limit shows in public pretrained models too: Mamba-130M copies a 32-word list 85% of the time, but 29% at 256 words and 7% at 1,000, while Pythia-160M stays at 86% to 93% (CPU, transformers v5.20.1).

11. Families and training objectives

The same blocks build three families, differing in which positions may see which, and in what they are trained to predict:

FamilyAttention maskObjectiveGood atExample
Decoder-onlyCausal: each token sees itself and earlier tokensPredict the next token at every positionGeneration; everything, at scaleGPT-3, Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek
Encoder-onlyBidirectional: every token sees every tokenRecover masked tokens (15% in BERT)Embeddings, classification, retrieval; cannot generate fluentlyBERT
Encoder-decoderBidirectional encoder over the input; causal decoder that also attends to itRebuild corrupted spans, or input-to-outputTranslation, summarisation; the input is encoded onceT5, T5Gemma 2

Decoder-only won because one objective, next-token prediction, turns any text into training data and any task into a prompt, and it scales simply. Two newer objectives change what a decoder predicts. Multi-token prediction (MTP) trains extra heads to predict tokens further ahead (Gloeckle et al. 2024): DeepSeek-V3 trains one extra token and can reuse that module as a draft for speculative decoding. Diffusion language models start from a fully masked sequence and unmask many tokens per step in any order, trading the strict left-to-right loop for parallel refinement (LLaDA, Nie et al. 2025; DiffusionGemma).

Measured on the tiny GPT (MTP lab of Families and objectives): one MTP module trained jointly lowers the main model's held-out loss from 2.278 to 2.241 at an equal number of tokens, a gain of 0.036; but the module adds 32% training FLOPs per step, and the plain model given those FLOPs reaches 2.160. At equal compute MTP loses at this scale. DeepSeek-V3 reports gains from MTP at a far larger scale (vendor), not tested here, and its module doubles as a draft for speculative decoding.

Go deeper (optional): Families and objectives owns the masks, the objectives, MTP and diffusion LMs; Pretraining how the objective is run at scale.

12. Reading a model's config in 30 seconds

A Hugging Face config.json is the architecture in about thirty fields. Read it with five questions, here on Llama 3.1 8B (excerpt, field order kept; full file):

"head_dim": 128, "hidden_act": "silu", "hidden_size": 4096, "intermediate_size": 14336, "max_position_embeddings": 131072, "num_attention_heads": 32, "num_hidden_layers": 32, "num_key_value_heads": 8, "rms_norm_eps": 1e-05, "rope_scaling": {"factor": 8.0, "high_freq_factor": 4.0, "low_freq_factor": 1.0, "original_max_position_embeddings": 8192, "rope_type": "llama3"}, "rope_theta": 500000.0, "tie_word_embeddings": false, "torch_dtype": "bfloat16", "vocab_size": 128256
  1. Shape: num_hidden_layers × hidden_size: 32 × 4,096.
  2. Attention and cache: num_attention_heads against num_key_value_heads: 32 against 8 is GQA with groups of 4; with head_dim 128 that is 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 128 KiB per token in BF16. Other variants announce themselves: kv_lora_rank and qk_rope_head_dim mean MLA, sliding_window or layer_types mean windowed layers, linear-layer fields mean a hybrid.
  3. FFN: intermediate_size 14,336 with silu means SwiGLU at 3.5d. MoE adds num_experts or n_routed_experts, num_experts_per_tok and a separate expert width (moe_intermediate_size).
  4. Position and context: rope_theta, rope_scaling and max_position_embeddings: trained at 8,192 and stretched 8 times to 131,072.
  5. Size: vocab_size and tie_word_embeddings for the embedding share, then section 8's formula: 8.03B.

Never derive head_dim as hidden_size / num_attention_heads when the field exists: Gemma 3 27B has hidden size 5,376 and 32 heads but head_dim 128, not 168 (config), and Qwen3-0.6B has 1,024 and 16 heads with head_dim 128 (config).

Go deeper (optional): paste any config into the Config calculator; the Architecture map lays these fields side by side for the models of the lineage; the LLM architecture gallery rebuilds them for many more.

13. Choosing: which design for which constraint

ConstraintChooseWhy, and what you give up
Short contexts, high throughput, standard serving stacksDense or MoE with GQA, SwiGLU, RoPE, pre-norm RMSNormMature kernels everywhere; the cache is small at short context anyway
Long contexts at high concurrencyMLA, or GQA with few KV heads; FP8 cache; windowed layers mixed with global onesShrinks what each token keeps or how long; costs kernel complexity (MLA) or far recall through fewer layers (windows)
Very long streams, fixed memoryHybrid: mostly SSM or linear layers, one attention layer in 4 to 8Near-constant memory; exact recall rests on the few attention layers
More quality at the same latency, memory availableMoE with many small experts and a shared expertActive parameters set latency; total parameters set memory, and balancing must be engineered
Small device, little memorySmall dense model, deep and thin, tied embeddings, GQAMoE does not help when every expert must fit in memory
Stable training at scalePre-norm RMSNorm plus QK-normTwo extra norms per layer, almost free

Go deeper (optional): the Architecture map lays these choices out model by model from GPT-2 to 2026 and has a picker by constraint: there DeepSeek-V3 keeps 68.6 KiB per token where Llama 3.1 405B keeps 504 KiB, and Gemma 3 27B's windows turn 62 GiB per 128K request into 10.4 GiB. The Config calculator checks a candidate: Llama 3.1 8B keeps 128 KiB per token, and its attention FLOPs equal its weight FLOPs at about 28,600 tokens of context. The LLM architecture gallery covers many more configs.

Common mistakes

Sizing the KV cache by query heads
The cache is set by KV heads. Llama 3.1 70B has 64 query heads and 8 KV heads; using 64 overstates its cache 8 times (2,560 KiB per token instead of 320).
Computing head_dim as hidden_size / num_heads
Gemma 3 27B: 5,376 / 32 = 168, but its head_dim is 128, so every derived cache and FLOP figure is 31% too high. Read the field when it exists (section 12).
Dropping rope_scaling when converting or copying a config
The model loads without a warning and answers short prompts well; past the original training length (8,192 for Llama 3.1) quality falls apart, because positions beyond it now get angles the model never saw. Diff the config against the original after any conversion. TODO 11 (labs): a real bad output from a run past the trained length, if a lab records one.
Treating total parameters as compute, or active parameters as memory
DeepSeek-V3 runs 37B parameters per token but needs memory for all 671B. Total sets the memory floor; active sets FLOPs per token. At large decode batches nearly every expert is touched in each step, so the weight bytes read per step approach the total, not the active count.
Assuming sparse attention or sliding windows shrink what a token stores
Selecting the top k keys cuts reads and FLOPs; every key is still stored for the indexer to choose from. A window caps how long entries are kept, not their size. Only fewer KV heads, compression (MLA), lower precision or layers without a cache shrink the per-token entry.
Calling a hybrid "cache-free"
Its attention layers still grow a cache (24 KiB per token in Qwen3-Next), and each request carries a fixed state for the recurrent layers.
Counting tied embeddings twice
With tie_word_embeddings: true the unembedding is the embedding matrix: count V × d once. For a 135M-parameter model with a 49,152-token vocabulary at d = 576 that is 28M parameters, a fifth of the model.

Interview questions

Parameters of a Llama 3.1 8B block, in your head?
Attention: Q and output 2 × 4,096² = 33.6M, K and V 2 × 4,096 × 1,024 = 8.4M; FFN 3 × 4,096 × 14,336 = 176.2M; about 218M. Times 32, plus two 525M embedding tables: 8.03B.
Why divide attention scores by √dh?
A dot product of two dh-dimensional vectors with unit-variance entries has variance dh. Without the scale, scores grow with head size, the softmax saturates into a one-hot and its gradients vanish.
Why is decode memory-bound when prefill is compute-bound?
Prefill multiplies every weight by thousands of prompt tokens at once: many FLOPs per byte read. Decode multiplies every weight, and reads the whole cache, for one new token per sequence: about 2 FLOPs per weight read. Batching more sequences raises the ratio for weights but not for each sequence's own cache.
GQA or MQA, and why not always MQA?
MQA has the smallest cache but the largest quality loss, and with tensor parallelism its single KV head must be replicated on every GPU. GQA with 8 groups keeps most of MHA's quality at an eighth (for 64 heads) of its cache, and 8 KV heads split cleanly over 8 GPUs.
Why pre-norm rather than the original post-norm?
Post-norm normalises the residual stream itself, so gradients to early layers pass through every norm and deep models need careful warmup. Pre-norm leaves an identity path from output to input; the price is a residual stream whose size grows with depth, which extra norms (QK-norm, norms after the sublayer) contain.
Your model is fine at 4K and produces garbage at 32K after a format conversion. First thing you check?
The RoPE fields: rope_theta, rope_scaling and max_position_embeddings against the original config. A dropped scaling rule is silent at short context.
Design: a model for 128K context that serves on one 80 GB GPU at batch 32.
Budget first: an 8B-class model's BF16 weights take about 16 GB, leaving about 64 GB for 32 × 131,072 = 4.2M cached tokens: about 15 KB per token across all layers. Llama 3.1 8B's GQA needs 128 KiB per token (512 GiB in total), 9 times over. So change the attention, not the size: for example 32 layers of which 8 are full attention with 2 KV heads of 128 and an FP8 cache (4 KiB per token, 16 GiB in total) and 24 linear or SSM layers (a fixed state of about 24 MiB per request, 768 MiB in total), leaving room for activations. Name the price: exact recall over 128K rests on 8 layers, so measure it with a long-context retrieval benchmark, and train the long-context phase with the target RoPE scaling. Alternatives to discuss: MLA (36 KiB per token at this shape in BF16, still too big alone at batch 32 without FP8 and fewer layers), or GQA with sliding windows on 5 of 6 layers (derived in src/read/derive.py).
Design: why did DeepSeek choose MLA, and what does it cost?
At DeepSeek-V3's shape (61 layers, 128 heads of 128) full MHA would keep 3,904 KiB per token; MLA keeps a 512-number latent plus a 64-number position key per layer, 68.6 KiB, 57 times less, which makes long-context serving of a large model affordable. DeepSeek reports quality at or above MHA in its ablations (DeepSeek-V2). The cost: extra projections in every attention call, a decoupled RoPE path because rotation cannot pass through the absorbed up-projections, its own kernels, and a cache that does not split across GPUs by heads (every head reads the same latent).
An MoE run's loss is fine but a third of the experts receive almost no tokens. What is happening and what do you change?
Routing collapse: early winners get more tokens, train faster and win more. Add or raise the load-balancing loss, or use bias-based balancing as in DeepSeek-V3; check the router's logits for growth (a router z-loss bounds them); log tokens per expert per layer from the start.

Block lab: one token through one decoder block

Every number a decoder block produces, for one real token of the running example, with the shape, the parameters and the FLOPs of each step, then where the compute goes as the context grows, and what happens to the residual stream (and to training) when the normalisation moves.

In one screenOne token, step by stepShape drillsWhere the FLOPs goPre-norm against post-normReal mistakesInterview questionsCode, runs and sources

In one screen

A decoder block is the unit a GPT repeats: it reads the residual stream (one vector of d_model numbers per token, the model’s working memory), lets the token gather information from earlier tokens (attention), transforms each token on its own (the feed-forward network, FFN), and adds both results back to the stream. The table lists every step with its output shape, its parameters and its forward FLOPs per token (a FLOP here is one multiply or one add, so a multiply-add of a weight costs 2). t is the number of positions the token attends to.

derived Real models from their config.json through the Config calculator’s code (window.CC); the tiny GPT from src/data/tiny_gpt.py (GPT-2 style: d_model 256, 6 layers, 8 heads of 32, LayerNorm pre-norm, GELU 4x FFN, learned positions, tied embeddings, no biases).

What the lab measured (Apple M1 Pro; the tiny GPT trained here in 5 minutes)
  • The FLOPs: PyTorch’s own counter on one forward pass of the 256-token running sequence gives 3,355,443,200 FLOPs, exactly the hand formula; a training step (forward and backward) counts 3.0x the forward, the origin of “6N per token”.
  • For the tiny GPT at context 256, the FFN is the largest cost per token (48%) and attention over the context 12%; for Llama 3.1 8B, decoding a token costs as much in attention as in all its weights at about 28.6k tokens of context.
  • The residual stream only grows under pre-norm: the traced token’s norm goes from 1.3 after the embedding to 65.8 after block 6 in the reference model; under post-norm it is reset to about 16 after every sub-layer.
  • Post-norm at the default learning rate (3e-3, 100 warmup steps) does not train: it stalls at the loss of a token-frequency model (5.943 against 6.006) because almost no gradient reaches its lower blocks (5.1e-7 at block 1). Pre-norm reaches 2.281 with the same settings; post-norm needs a lower rate or a 500-step warmup, with which it reaches 2.138, the best of eight runs.

One token through one block, step by step

The token is “o” at position 157 of the running sequence, in ““Why are you sad, Ro”. The trained tiny GPT (the reference run, held-out loss 2.28) gives the next token, “x”, a probability of 75.8%: it has to find “Roxy” earlier in the story and copy it, which is attention’s job. Every picture below is the real vector at that step, one cell per number (orange positive, blue negative, darker is larger in magnitude), recorded by src/block/trace.py, which re-runs the block step by step and checks that its logits equal the model’s own forward pass (largest difference 1.5e-5). The model selector changes the shapes, parameter counts and FLOPs to a real model’s; the pictures and measured values stay the tiny GPT’s.

The same step in transformers’ Llama code (v5.20.1)

    What the recorded weights show (softmax step): in block 1, heads 1, 6 and 7 look mostly at the previous token, “R” (weights 0.65, 0.70 and 0.31), and head 5 already puts 0.39 on the “x” of the last “Roxy” (position 143). In blocks 5 and 6, several heads park 0.89 to 0.98 of their weight on the opening quote mark (position 150), a sink-like habit, and block 5’s head 4 has its largest weight (0.13) on the “x” of the very first “Roxy” (position 22). The Inside a real model tab measures such heads properly (induction scores, sinks) on SmolLM2-135M.

    Why each design choice exists. The scale 1/√d_head: a dot product of two vectors of d_head independent entries with variance 1 has variance d_head, so without the scale the softmax saturates (one weight near 1, gradients near 0) more as heads get wider. Softmax makes the weights positive and sum to one, so the head reads an average whose size does not depend on how many tokens it sees. Several heads let one layer look for several things at once (here one head copies the name, others track nearby words) at the same cost as one wide head. The residual add keeps an identity path from the embedding to the output, so a block only has to learn a correction and gradients reach the first layer. The FFN’s 4x width is the 2017 Transformer’s choice (d_model 512, d_ff 2048); SwiGLU uses three matrices, so Llama-style models cut the width to about 8/3 x d_model to keep the same parameters (Llama 3.1 8B: 14,336 / 4,096 = 3.5, a little wider).

    Go deeper (optional): The transformer from zero derives each step and trains the GPT; Attention variants and the Attention lab change what each token stores; Positional encodings owns RoPE; Activation functions owns GELU and SwiGLU.

    Shape drills: predict, then reveal

    1. Llama 3.1 8B: what is the shape of k_proj.weight? (hidden_size 4,096; 32 heads; 8 KV heads; head_dim 128)
    Skip to the answer
    (1024, 4096). K has num_key_value_heads x head_dim = 8 x 128 = 1,024 outputs, and nn.Linear(in, out) stores its weight as (out, in). q_proj is (4096, 4096). The tempting (4096, 4096) is right for multi-head attention, where K has as many heads as Q; grouped-query attention is why Llama’s K and V are 4x smaller than Q (modeling_llama.py:219-227).
    2. The tiny GPT runs the 256-token sequence with eager attention. What is the shape of one layer’s attention weights, and how many bytes in float32?
    Skip to the answer
    (batch, heads, T, T) = (1, 8, 256, 256): 524,288 numbers, 2 MiB in float32, per layer. It grows with T squared: at T = 32,768 one Llama 3.1 8B layer (32 heads) would need 32 x 32,768² x 2 bytes = 64 GiB in bfloat16 for one sequence. That is why fused kernels (FlashAttention) compute the softmax tile by tile and never store this tensor (CUDA: writing kernels). The heads come before T because .view(B, T, H, hd).transpose(1, 2) moves them there (option 4 is the shape before the transpose).
    3. Decoding one token at context 256, which operation of the tiny GPT costs the most FLOPs?
    Skip to the answer
    The FFN: 6,291,456 of 13,107,200 FLOPs (48%). Then the unembedding 2,097,152 (16%; the vocabulary is 16x d_model), Q, K, V 2,359,296 (18%), attention over the context 1,572,864 (12%) and the output projection 786,432 (6%). Attention passes the FFN only past 4 x 256 = 1,024 positions here (its cost is 4 x d x t per layer against 16 x d² for the FFN). Move the context slider in Where the FLOPs go to see it.

    Where the FLOPs go: 2N, 6N and the attention term

    The problem. “How much compute does a model need per token?” decides training budgets and serving cost, and it has a two-line answer once the block is clear. How it works. A weight matrix of shape (out, in) applied to one token is out x in multiply-adds, 2 x out x in FLOPs. Every matrix weight a token passes through is used exactly once, so the weights cost 2N FLOPs, N being the matrix weights a token touches (the input embedding is a row copy and costs nothing; a tied LM head is a matrix product and counts; in a mixture of experts only the active experts count). Attention adds work no weight accounts for: per layer, the query meets t keys (2 x d_attn x t) and the weights meet t values (the same again), so 4 x n_layer x d_attn x t for a token that sees t positions. The backward pass needs two products of the same size per weight (the gradient for the input and the gradient for the weight), so a training step is about 3x the forward: 6N per token when attention is small.

    forward per token = 2N + 4 x n_layer x d_attn x t (t = positions attended) training per token = 3 x forward ~ 6N when 4 x n_layer x d_attn x t is small next to 2N

    measured PyTorch’s FLOP counter (torch.utils.flop_counter.FlopCounterMode, torch 2.14.1, CPU) on one forward pass of the tiny GPT over the 256-token running sequence: 3,355,443,200 FLOPs, equal to the formula (2N x 256 = 2,952,790,016 for the weights plus 402,653,184 for attention), and the same exact match for the SwiGLU and GQA presets. Forward plus backward on 255 tokens: 10,022,307,840 against 3,340,769,280 forward, a ratio of 3.0. The counter sees the full 256 x 256 score matrix (the mask is added, nothing is skipped), so its attention term is t = 256 for every token; a causal kernel such as FlashAttention skips the masked half, which is the per-token average of t(t+1)/2 / t that the calculator uses for prefill. Script: src/block/flops.py.

    published Kaplan et al. 2020, Table 1 (arXiv 2001.08361, read 2026-10-18), writes C_forward = 2N + 2 n_layer n_ctx d_attn with N the non-embedding parameters, and drops the context term because it is “a relatively small fraction” when d_model > n_ctx / 12; with the backward pass “approximately twice the compute”, C ≈ 6N. Their single context term equals the two products here averaged over a causal context (each sees n_ctx/2 positions on average). Their N also leaves out the de-embedding (LM head), which they count apart (2 d_model n_vocab); the calculator below keeps it in 2N, which matters for small models with large vocabularies.

    FLOPs per token by operation, against context

    256 tokens

    derived from each model’s config.json with the Config calculator’s formulas (window.CC: sliding-window layers stop at their window, MLA decodes in the absorbed form, recurrent layers counted per step); this card only splits CC’s weight FLOPs by operation, and the check line confirms the split adds back to CC’s 2N. Decode: the token at position t reads t cached positions. Prefill: the average over a t-token prompt. The solid line is the slider; the dashed line is where attention over the context equals 2N.

    When it matters. For the tiny GPT (d_model 256) attention reaches 2N at 1,878 positions when decoding (3,754 averaged over a prefill); for Llama 3.1 8B (d_attn 4,096) at 28,628 (57,255); for a model whose attention layers all use a window (or for an SSM) the line never comes. A decoder-only layer of width d with a 4x FFN has 12 d² matrix weights (4 d² attention, 8 d² FFN), 24 d² FLOPs, against 4 d t for attention, so for the blocks alone the crossover is t = 6 d for one decoded token and t = 12 d averaged over a causal prefill, Kaplan’s n_ctx / 12 rule; the LM head and a wider FFN push it later. GQA does not move it: it shrinks K and V, not the queries that do the dot products. How to check. Wrap one forward in FlopCounterMode (it counts matrix products only) on the eager path, or compare a profiler’s matmul time to its attention-kernel time at two context lengths. What transfers. FLOP counts are properties of the architecture and transfer exactly; time does not, because decoding is limited by memory traffic (weights and KV cache read per token), not by FLOPs (Performance math).

    Pre-norm against post-norm: the same token, the same seed, the same budget

    The problem. A stack of blocks is hard to train when the size of the activations or the gradients changes from layer to layer. Normalisation fixes the size of a vector; the question is where to put it. Post-norm (the 2017 Transformer, BERT) normalises after the residual add, x ← Norm(x + F(x)): the stream itself is rescaled at every sub-layer. Pre-norm (GPT-2 onward, every current LLM) normalises only the copy the sub-layer reads, x ← x + F(Norm(x)), and leaves the stream alone, so there is an untouched identity path from the embedding to the last block. The tiny GPT has both as a switch (norm_pos); everything else (seed, data order, schedule, 1,500 steps of 8,192 tokens) is equal.

    Residual-stream norm after each sub-layer: pre-norm against post-norm

    pre-norm
    post-norm

    measured With both models trained at the same learning rate (1e-3, the highest where post-norm trains with the default 100-step warmup), the traced token’s stream grows from 0.9 after the embedding to 14.8 after block 6 under pre-norm, and stays between 16.0 and 16.4 under post-norm (√256 = 16 times a gain near 1) until the last norm, whose learned gain takes it to 24.6. The trained reference model of the walkthrough (pre-norm, lr 3e-3) grows from 1.3 to 65.8, most of it in block 1’s FFN (a branch of norm 53.0). That growth is the cost of pre-norm: later blocks add updates that are small next to the stream, so each layer changes the representation less (one argument for the depth-scaled initialisations and the extra norms of newer models), and the final norm (ln_f in the tiny GPT, self.norm at modeling_llama.py:402) is mandatory.

    Held-out loss at five learning rates (1,500 steps each)

    Thick lines: held-out loss every 100 steps (20 fixed validation windows). Thin lines: training loss every 20 steps. Dashed: the loss of a model that ignores context and predicts each token by its frequency in the training shard (6.01 nats on the held-out split; ln 4,096 = 8.32 is a uniform guess).

    measured At the default learning rate 3e-3 with a 100-step warmup, post-norm fails: by step 30 its training loss is at the unigram level (6.04) and it ends at 5.943, while pre-norm reaches 2.281 with identical settings. Lower the learning rate and post-norm trains (2.534 at 1e-3, 3.215 at 3e-4); keep 3e-3 but warm up over 500 steps and it reaches 2.138, the best of the eight runs. Pre-norm trains at every rate tried, degrading gracefully: 2.464 at 1e-3, 2.734 at 1e-2, 4.361 at 3e-2, where its gradient norm (before clipping) spikes to 40.8. That is the trade in one chart: pre-norm is forgiving, post-norm can be better but only inside a narrow window of learning rate and warmup.

    Gradient norm reaching each block

    Norm of the gradient of all a block’s parameters, one backward pass on 8 fixed held-out windows of 256 tokens, log scale (src/block/gradnorm.py, CPU).

    measured Why the failed run failed: after training, the gradient reaching block 1 of the post-norm model at lr 3e-3 is 5.1e-7, against 0.027 at block 6, a factor of about 50,000. Its lower blocks stopped learning; the model that remains predicts token frequencies. The runs that trained (post-norm at 1e-3 or with the long warmup, pre-norm) have block gradients between 0.27 and 0.92, roughly even across depth.

    Does not reproduce at this depth: Xiong et al. 2020, Figure 3
    Xiong et al. (arXiv 2002.04745) show that at initialisation post-norm’s gradients grow toward the output layers while pre-norm’s stay level, and derive that a warmup is needed for post-norm. In this 6-layer model at initialisation, post-norm’s block gradients are level (0.074 to 0.075) and 20 to 30x smaller than pre-norm’s, which decrease slightly with depth (2.21 at block 1 to 1.57 at block 6). Their warmup conclusion does reproduce (the 500-step warmup rescues lr 3e-3); the depth profile likely needs a deeper stack to appear. Not run here: a 24-layer version.

    When it matters. Post-norm’s fragility grows with depth, which is why it vanished from LLMs; pre-norm’s stream growth is what newer recipes tame with QK-norm, sandwich norms (Gemma 2 and 3) and depth-scaled initialisation (Normalisation, residuals and stability owns those). How to check a run. Log the per-block gradient norm and the residual-stream norm per layer (one forward with hooks, as in trace.py); a training loss that sits at the unigram entropy of your data, with a small, flat gradient norm, is a model that stopped using context.

    Real mistakes in a hand-written block

    Four one-line bugs that a from-scratch attention commonly has, each run on the trained tiny GPT with the running sequence (src/block/mistakes.py, CPU). None of them raises an error: the model still produces fluent-looking text, and only the loss shows the damage. That is the case for always checking a rewritten block against a reference forward (here: the rewritten correct forward reproduces the model’s loss exactly, 1.96).

    The missing mask does not change the last position (it has no future to see) but corrupts every earlier position’s keys and values from block 2 on, so even generation changes. The missing scale is the mildest here because d_head is only 32 (scores 5.7x too large in spread); at d_head 128 the softmax saturates harder. Splitting heads with .view(B, H, T, hd) cuts the sequence into head-sized slices: shapes are legal and nothing complains.

    And the errors that do raise, verbatim (scrubbed of paths), with what each means:

    In order: the learned position table has 256 rows, so position 256 does not exist (an RoPE model would run and degrade instead, see Positional encodings); GPTConfig asserts that d_model splits evenly into heads; q @ k without .transpose(-2, -1) multiplies (256 x 32) by (256 x 32); and K, V with fewer heads than Q need repeat_kv (or an attention kernel that supports grouped heads) before the product.

    Interview questions

    Count the parameters of one Llama 3.1 8B block from its config, in your head.

    d = 4,096, 32 query heads and 8 KV heads of 128, FFN 14,336. Attention: Q and O are d x d each (2 x 16.8M), K and V are d x 1,024 each (2 x 4.2M): 41.9M. SwiGLU FFN: 3 x 4,096 x 14,336 = 176.2M. Two RMSNorm gains: 8,192. Block: 218.1M; x 32 = 6.98B; plus untied embedding and LM head, 2 x 128,256 x 4,096 = 1.05B: 8,030,261,248, the Hub’s exact count (the Config calculator reproduces it).

    Forward and training FLOPs per token, and the training compute for D tokens?

    Forward 2N + 4 x n_layer x d_attn x t; training about 3x that, 6N when context is short. Training compute about 6 x N x D. For Llama 3.1 8B (N = 7.50B matrix weights including the LM head) over an illustrative 15 trillion tokens: 6 x 7.50e9 x 1.5e13 = 6.8e23 FLOPs (calculated). Measured here: a training step counts exactly 3.0x the forward.

    Llama 3.1 8B decodes token 131,072. Where does its compute go?

    2N = 15.0 GFLOPs for the weights; attention over the context 4 x 32 x 4,096 x 131,072 = 68.7 GFLOPs, 4.6x the weights (calculated with the Config calculator’s formulas). GQA does not reduce this (32 query heads still do the dot products); it reduces the KV bytes read, which is what limits decode speed. Only windows, sparse or latent attention, or fewer attention layers (hybrids) cut the FLOPs.

    Why divide the scores by √d_head? What breaks without it?

    q · k sums d_head products; with unit-variance entries its variance is d_head. The softmax of large scores is nearly one-hot, its gradient nearly zero, so learning stalls, more so for wider heads. Measured here on the trained tiny GPT: removing the scale raises the loss on the running sequence from 1.96 to 2.88.

    Pre-norm or post-norm? What does each cost?

    Post-norm (2017 Transformer, BERT) normalises the stream after each add: activations stay bounded, but gradients to early layers pass through every norm and shrink, and deep models need a warmup and a lower learning rate. Pre-norm (GPT-2 onward) normalises only the sub-layer’s input: an identity path from embedding to output, stable at higher learning rates, but the stream’s norm grows with depth and a final norm is required before the LM head. Measured here: see the section above.

    Why is the FFN 4x wide, and why is SwiGLU’s 8/3?

    4x is the 2017 Transformer’s d_ff = 2,048 for d_model = 512, kept since. A two-matrix FFN of width 4d has 8 d² weights; SwiGLU has three matrices, so width 8/3 d gives the same 8 d² (Shazeer 2020, arXiv 2002.05202). Models then round for hardware: the tiny GPT’s SwiGLU preset uses 704 (8/3 x 256 rounded up to 32), Llama 3.1 8B uses 14,336 = 3.5 x 4,096.

    Design: a model must answer 32k-token prompts cheaply. Which parts of the block would you change, and what does each cost?

    Measure first: at 32k context a Llama-8B-shaped model spends about as much on attention as on all its weights in prefill (crossover 57,255 averaged over a prompt, 28,628 for decode), and decode time is set by bytes read (weights plus KV cache), not FLOPs. Levers: GQA or MLA cut KV bytes (decode speed, batch size) but not FLOPs; sliding-window layers interleaved with a few global ones (Gemma 3, 5:1) cut both, at a cost in long-range recall; replacing most attention layers with SSM layers (hybrids) makes most of the model’s cost independent of context, at a cost in exact copying; a smaller vocabulary or a tied head trims the fixed 2 x d x V. Check each with the Attention lab and the Config calculator, then on a long-context benchmark.

    What transfers to a datacenter model. Shapes, parameter counts and FLOP counts transfer exactly (they are arithmetic on the config). Residual-norm growth under pre-norm and post-norm’s sensitivity to the learning rate are general (Xiong et al. 2020; the post-norm failure threshold depends on depth, width, optimiser and warmup, so the exact learning rates here do not transfer).     Sources. Vaswani et al. 2017, Attention Is All You Need (d_ff = 2,048 for d_model = 512, post-norm, the √d_k scale); Kaplan et al. 2020, Table 1 and section 2.1 (arXiv 2001.08361); Xiong et al. 2020, On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture (arXiv 2002.04745); Shazeer 2020, GLU Variants Improve Transformer (arXiv 2002.05202); transformers v5.20.1 (commit 0ea8779) models/llama/modeling_llama.py; configs as recorded in src/data/configs/. All read 2026-10-18.

    Every attention variant answers one question differently: what must each token leave behind so that later tokens can read it? That leftover, the KV cache, decides how much memory a long conversation takes and how many bytes each generated token has to read, and those two numbers usually decide the serving bill. This tab builds the cache from first principles on the running example, runs the same sequence through MHA, GQA, MQA, MLA and a sliding window with each token's entry drawn to scale, trains the variants on one budget, times the decode step on an Apple M1 Pro, and ends with a calculator that sizes the cache of any real model for a serving budget.

    1. Why a cache2. Four caches, one sequence3. Trained on one budget4. Published ablations5. Decode speed6. Windows and sinks7. Sparse attention8. Size a cache9. Drills, mistakes, interviews10. The code

    Labels: measured run here on an Apple M1 Pro; published from a paper or model card (vendor or independent said beside it); derived computed from a config with the formula shown; illustrative chosen to show a mechanism. Reading time about 24 minutes, plus about 10 in closed details (tables and code skimmed).

    1. Why attention keeps a cache

    The problem. A decoder generates one token at a time. At step t the new token's query must be compared with the key of every earlier token, and the resulting weights average the earlier tokens' values. Keys and values are projections of each token's residual stream at that layer (k = WKx, v = WVx), and a token's x at a layer never changes once it is computed, because causal attention never lets a token see later ones. So recomputing them at every step is pure waste: step t would redo t projections per layer, and generating n tokens would cost about n2/2 projections instead of n.

    How it works. Each layer stores every token's keys and values the first time it computes them and appends one entry per new token. Decoding then costs one new key and value per layer plus a read of everything stored. That read is the catch: the cache is read in full for every generated token, and at batch sizes that fit in memory the decode step is limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic (the case is made with numbers on Performance math).

    KV bytes per token = 2 (K and V) x layers x KV heads x head_dim x bytes per number tiny GPT, MHA: 2 x 6 x 8 x 32 x 2 (bf16) = 6,144 bytes per token -> 1.5 MiB at its 256-token context Llama 3.1 8B: 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 bytes (128 KiB) -> 16 GiB at 131,072 tokens, per sequence

    derived Formula and shapes from the configs in src/data/ (tiny GPT, tiny_gpt.py kv_cache_bytes_per_token) and Llama 3.1 8B's config.json (32 layers, 8 KV heads of 128; read 2026-10-18). bf16 throughout, as in the Config calculator and the Architecture map.

    What it costs, when it matters. The cache grows linearly with context and with batch, and for every token decoded the whole thing streams through the chip. At short context and small batch the weights dominate memory traffic; at long context or large batch the cache does (the Config calculator finds Llama 3.1 8B's attention reads equal its weight reads at about 28,600 cached tokens). Every variant below shrinks one factor of the formula: GQA and MQA shrink "KV heads", MLA replaces "2 x KV heads x head_dim" by one small latent, sliding windows cap the number of tokens a layer keeps, sparse attention keeps everything but reads only part of it, and state-space layers keep a fixed-size state instead (the Reading tab's section 10).

    How to check it. Count it from the config (the formula above, or section 8), then confirm in the serving engine's startup log, which reports the KV cache memory and the number of tokens it can hold (vLLM prints both); the two disagree when the engine pads blocks or the config has windows you did not credit.

    2. Four caches, one sequence

    The same 16 tokens, the opening of the running sequence ("Once upon a time, in a big forest, there lived a rhinoceros"), decoded one at a time by the tiny GPT. The top panel is plain multi-head attention, the method every variant replaced; the bottom panel is the variant you pick. Both are drawn to one scale: one square is 16 numbers cached for one token in one layer, so area is memory. Under each panel, the 8 query heads of the current token are coloured by the KV head they read.

    Shapes are the tiny GPT's presets (src/data/configs.py): 6 layers, 8 query heads of 32. GQA-4 and GQA-2 keep 4 and 2 KV heads, MQA one; MLA caches a 64-number latent plus a 16-number position key; the sliding window is drawn as 8 tokens illustrative so eviction is visible in 16 steps (the trained preset uses 64, and at its 256-token context keeps a quarter of the full cache on average). Byte counters are bf16 and agree with kv_cache_bytes_per_token in tiny_gpt.py.

    What the picture says.

    • MHA (multi-head attention, Vaswani et al. 2017): each query head has its own key and value head, so each token stores 2 x 8 x 32 = 512 numbers per layer.
    • GQA (grouped-query attention, Ainslie et al. 2023): query heads share K and V in groups. GQA-2 keeps 2 KV heads, each read by 4 query heads: a quarter of the cache. Queries keep full resolution, so heads can still look at different things, but heads in one group must look through the same keys.
    • MQA (multi-query attention, Shazeer 2019): the limit, one KV head shared by all 8 query heads, an eighth of the cache.
    • MLA (multi-head latent attention, DeepSeek-V2): the token stores one compressed latent and one small position key shared by all heads; per-head keys and values are rebuilt from the latent by up-projections (or absorbed into the query and output at decode, so they are never materialised). Here 64 + 16 = 80 numbers instead of 512, between MQA and GQA-2 in size, but every head gets its own keys. How the compression, the decoupled RoPE key and the absorption work is animated step by step on DeepSeek and derived in section 3 of Attention variants; this lab does not repeat it.
    • Sliding window (Mistral 7B, Gemma 3, gpt-oss): what each token stores is unchanged; the layer simply forgets tokens older than the window. It caps the cache instead of shrinking each entry, and it changes what the model can see (section 6).

    3. The variants trained on one budget

    Pictures of caches say nothing about quality. So each variant of the tiny GPT was trained from scratch with the same seed, the same 1,500 batches (12.3M tokens of TinyStories), the same learning-rate schedule and RoPE positions everywhere (the setup's baseline uses learned positions and its MLA preset uses RoPE, so the comparison would otherwise mix two changes). Held-out loss is the mean cross-entropy on 3,200 fixed validation windows of 256 tokens (eval.py); lower is better, and ln 4,096 = 8.32 is a model that knows nothing.

    Loss curves, same batches

    Greedy continuations of two evaluation prompts, per variant

    4. What the published ablations say

    A 6M-parameter model trained for five minutes cannot show the quality differences that appear at billions of parameters and trillions of tokens. Two papers trained variants that differ only in attention at real scale; both are the authors' own runs, and both compare on benchmarks rather than loss.

    5. Decode speed: the cache is what the step reads

    The claim to test. At decode, every new token's attention reads the whole cache once. If that read is memory-bound, the time of the attention step should scale with the bytes cached, not with the number of query heads or the FLOPs. One attention layer at Llama 3.1 8B's shape (32 query heads of 128, batch 4, fp16) was timed on the M1 Pro's GPU for each variant, with the cache sized to each context.

    The whole tiny GPT, one decode step

    6. Sliding windows, local and global layers, and attention sinks

    The problem a window solves. GQA and MLA make each entry smaller; the cache still grows with every token. A sliding window of W tokens caps it: a layer keeps only the last W entries, in a ring buffer ("the keys and values for the timestep i are stored in position i mod W of the cache", Mistral 7B, section 2). Information older than W can still travel, one window per layer: "hi can access tokens from the input layer at a distance of up to W x k tokens", about 131K for W = 4,096 over 32 layers (same source, vendor). That is a theoretical span: the information has to be relayed through intermediate tokens, and nothing guarantees a model learns to do it.

    Local and global layers. Every recent design that uses windows keeps some full layers, so that long-range retrieval has a direct path. Gemma 3 uses "a pattern of 5 local layers for every global layer" with a span of "only 1024 tokens" for the local layers, introduced because of "the memory explosion of the KV cache" at 128K (Gemma 3 report, vendor). gpt-oss alternates "banded window and fully dense patterns, where the bandwidth is 128 tokens" (gpt-oss model card, vendor). Calculated from their configs with windows credited, at 131,072 tokens in bf16 derived: Gemma 3 27B stores 496 KiB per token by the formula but holds 10.41 GiB per sequence, against 62.00 GiB if all 62 layers were global; gpt-oss-120b holds 4.50 GiB against 9.00 GiB; Mistral 7B v0.1, whose 32 layers all use a 4,096-token window, holds 0.50 GiB against 16.00 GiB (the same arithmetic as the Architecture map).

    Attention sinks. Softmax weights must sum to one, so a head with nothing relevant to read still has to put its attention somewhere; trained models learn to park it on the first token, whatever that token is (StreamingLLM, Xiao et al. 2023). A sliding cache that evicts the first token removes the parking place, and the model breaks. The fix is to keep a few initial tokens forever, or to train with an explicit sink: gpt-oss gives "each attention head ... a learned bias in the denominator of the softmax ... which enables the attention mechanism to pay no attention to any tokens" (model card, vendor; the tiny GPT has the same switch as attn_sink). The Inside a real model tab measures sinks in SmolLM2-135M; here the question is what they mean for a cache.

    Before and after: one trained model, served with a sliding cache

    The full-attention MHA model of section 3 (trained on 256-token windows) is served as if its cache were a sliding window of W tokens: first evicting everything older than W, then keeping the first token (or the first four) as StreamingLLM does. The SWA-64 model, trained with its window, is the control. Loss is counted only at positions at or beyond W, where something has been evicted.

    7. Sparse attention: keep everything, read a little

    The problem. Windows forget; GQA and MLA still read every cached token at every step. Sparse attention keeps the whole cache but lets each query read only a chosen subset, which cuts decode reads and long-context FLOPs while leaving storage as it was. The hard part is choosing the subset cheaply and learning to choose it during training ("natively trainable"), rather than pruning a dense model afterwards.

    • NSA (Native Sparse Attention, Yuan et al. 2025, DeepSeek-AI and Peking University): three branches per query, "compressed coarse-grained tokens, selectively retained fine-grained tokens, and sliding windows for local contextual information", combined by learned gates, with kernels that load blocks of keys. Its Table 4 counts what one decode step must load:
    • DSA (DeepSeek Sparse Attention, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, then V3.2): a "lightning indexer" with a few heads scores every cached token for each query (ReLU scores, "can be implemented in FP8"), and the MLA attention then reads only the top-k entries. DeepSeek: DSA "reduces the core attention complexity of the main model from O(L2) to O(Lk)", while "the lightning indexer still has a complexity of O(L2)" but needs much less compute (DeepSeek-V3.2 technical report, section 2, vendor). The V3.2 config sets index_topk 2,048, index_n_heads 64 and index_head_dim 128 (read 2026-10-18). At 131,072 cached tokens a query reads 2,048 full entries, 1.6% of them, but the indexer still scores all 131,072 with its 128-number keys, so the read per step is smaller, not constant (derived). DeepSeek says it "deliberately aligned the training configurations of DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp with V3.1-Terminus" and reports "performance on par with V3.1-Terminus" (model card, vendor; how long-context quality is measured independently is on Long-context and multimodal benchmarks).

    When it matters, how to check. Sparse attention pays at long context (tens of thousands of tokens and up), where the read of the cache dominates the step; at 4K it mostly adds an indexer. Check by measuring decode time per token against context in the serving engine with the sparse kernels enabled, and by a long-context retrieval benchmark rather than perplexity, since a selector that misses the one needed token barely moves average loss. Not run here: both need CUDA kernels (FlashMLA, DeepGEMM) and models far beyond this Mac.

    Go deeper: Attention variants derives each variant, sinks and sparse attention in depth; Long context covers what windows and sparsity do to long-context quality; Batching, KV cache and scheduling and PagedAttention cover how engines store and share the cache.

    8. Size the cache of a real model for a serving budget

    The question a serving design starts from: how many sequences of this length fit on this GPU? Pick a model (configs read from the Hugging Face Hub on 2026-10-18, the same files and formulas as the Config calculator), a context, a batch and the number formats. The "what if" table re-runs the same model with its attention swapped, keeping everything else, so you can see what GQA, MQA or an MLA-sized latent would have bought it.

    derived KV bytes = sum over attention layers of 2 x KV heads x head_dim x min(context, window) x bytes (MLA: (latent + RoPE key + indexer key) x context x bytes); state-space layers add a fixed state per sequence (fp32, as the calculator assumes). Windows are credited: a sliding layer holds at most its window. Weights = total parameters x the chosen bytes. GPU memory in GB (109 bytes), cache in GiB (230). Ten per cent of the GPU is held back for activations, the CUDA context and fragmentation illustrative; real engines reserve a configurable share (vLLM's gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 0.9). "What if" rows: MHA = one KV head per query head; GQA-8 = 8 KV heads; MQA = one; MLA = DeepSeek-V3's 512-number latent plus 64-number RoPE key in every attention layer; head_dim kept (for MLA models converted to MHA, head_dim = v_head_dim, DeepSeek's own convention).

    Every model's attention, read from its config

    Tap a row to load it in the calculator above. KV per token is the full per-token cost in bf16, summed over the attention layers; the last column credits windows at 131,072 tokens (a model whose context is shorter would never hold that much; the column compares designs, not products).
