    Common mistakes

    Interview questions

    Why does decoding need a KV cache, and why is a decode step memory-bound?
    A token's keys and values at a layer never change in a causal decoder, so they are computed once and stored; without the cache, step t recomputes t projections per layer. With it, each step does a little arithmetic per byte read: each cached number (2 bytes in bf16) is multiplied and added once by each query head that shares it, so attention does about (query heads / KV heads) FLOPs per byte read: 1 for MHA, 4 for Llama 3's GQA, and batching does not raise it because every sequence has its own cache. A datacenter GPU needs hundreds of FLOPs per byte to be compute-bound (Performance math), so the step waits on memory. Section 5 measures it.
    Compute the KV cache of Llama 3.1 70B for one 128K-token request.
    GQA, MQA or MLA: what does each give up?
    GQA shares keys and values inside groups of query heads: a small quality cost, no new parts, every kernel supports it (DeepSeek's 7B ablation still shows GQA-8 below MHA on hard benchmarks, section 4). MQA is the extreme: the largest saving and the largest quality cost, and with tensor parallelism the single KV head is replicated on every GPU, so the per-GPU saving shrinks. MLA stores a compressed latent: the cache of a few KV heads with quality at or above MHA in DeepSeek's runs, paid for with extra projections, a decoupled RoPE key, custom kernels and, because the latent is shared by all heads, no way to split the cache across tensor-parallel ranks by head (derived from the design). GQA is the default when you want boring; MLA when the cache dominates the bill.
    Why does MLA need a separate RoPE key?
    At decode, MLA folds the key up-projection into the query (absorption), so attention runs directly against the cached latent. RoPE rotates keys by a position-dependent matrix that would sit between the up-projection and the query, and a matrix that changes with position cannot be folded into a fixed one. So the position information gets its own small key (64 numbers in DeepSeek-V3), shared by all heads and cached beside the latent, while the latent part carries no rotation. The step-by-step version is on DeepSeek.
    Design: a model for 128K context that serves 32 sequences on one 80 GB GPU.
    Why did DeepSeek choose MLA, and what does it cost?
    Sliding window or sparse attention for long context?
    A window caps memory and reads but forgets: anything older than the window must be relayed through layers, which models often fail to learn, so designs keep some global layers (Gemma 3 1 in 6, gpt-oss 1 in 2). Sparse attention (NSA, DSA) keeps everything and reads a learned subset, so it can still retrieve one old token, but the cache is as large as before and the selector costs something at every step. Windows when memory is the limit, sparse attention when reads and long-range recall both matter, and often both together with GQA or MLA underneath.
    A model breaks when you serve it with a rolling cache. Why, and what is the fix?

    10. The code

    Every number in this tab came from the scripts in src/attn/ and the shared tiny GPT in src/data/. The cache is a few lines; the quotes from transformers are at the pinned v5.20.1, located by pattern (src/attn/extract_code.py).

    How the runs were made, and how to rerun them

    Training (MPS, under the shared bench lock, one run at a time): train.py --preset <p> --set pos=rope --steps 1500 then eval.py, for rope (MHA), gqa4, gqa2, mqa, mla, swa64, swa64_g3, with seed 1 repeats of MHA, MQA and MLA. Queue script: src/attn/run_train.sh; results summarised into src/attn/out/runs_summary.json by make_page_data.py.

    Decode timing: src/attn/decode_bench.py (MPS, about two minutes) writes out/decode_bench.json. Serving with a sliding cache, sinks, the GQA expansion bug: src/attn/cpu_evals.py (CPU, a few minutes) writes out/cpu_evals.json. Error messages: src/attn/sdpa_errors.py. Page data: make_page_data.py writes parts/32_js_at_0data.js; check_data.py checks the page against the recorded files.

    A model's config.json is enough to know how many parameters it has, how many it uses per token, how many floating-point operations (FLOPs) each token costs, and how much memory its weights and its cache take. This tab does that arithmetic with one set of formulas, shows the formulas with the chosen model's numbers in them, and checks them against the exact stored tensor counts of real checkpoints.

    Pick a modelWhere the parameters liveThe formulasContext lengthDense vs MoEIn your headCheckedMistakesInterviewThe code
    Words used on this tab
    Parameter: one trainable number (a weight, a bias or a norm gain). Total parameters: all of them, which is what must sit in memory. Active parameters: the ones one token actually multiplies through; smaller than the total only in a mixture of experts (MoE), where a router sends each token to k of E expert feed-forward blocks. FLOP: one floating-point add or multiply; a multiply-add is 2 FLOPs, so a token through a weight matrix with P entries costs 2P FLOPs. KV cache: the keys and values of every earlier token, kept so each new token does not recompute them; its size grows with the context. Prefill: processing the prompt (all its tokens at once); decode: generating one new token at a time against the cache. Shapes: d = hidden size (hidden_size), V = vocabulary, nh query heads, nkv key/value heads, dh head dimension, f feed-forward width (intermediate_size), L layers.

    Pick a model, or paste a config

    Paste your own config.json

    Any Hugging Face config of a supported family: Llama, Mistral, Mixtral, Qwen2/3 and Qwen3-MoE, Qwen3-Next, Gemma 1/2/3, Phi-3/4, OLMo 2/3, GPT-2, gpt-oss, Llama 4, DeepSeek-V2/V3/V3.2, Kimi K2, GLM-4.5, MiniMax-M2, Nemotron-H (dense layers, from hybrid_override_pattern or layers_block_type), Granite 4.0-H, Falcon-H1, Jamba, Mamba and Mamba-2. Refused with a reason rather than miscounted: GLM-5 (glm_moe_dsa), DeepSeek-V4, Kimi Linear and Kimi K3 (kimi_linear), Gemma 4, and Nemotron 3's MoE layers; the Architecture map shows their layouts and caches. Llama 4 Scout's config has an empty no_rope_layers, so it is treated as all-global here (transformers fills in one NoPE global layer in 4; see the note under the model). Edit a number (try num_key_value_heads) and press Compute.

    Where the parameters live

    Both bars are drawn to the same scale: the top one is everything that must be in memory, the bottom one is what a single token multiplies through. For a dense model they are the same length. For an MoE model the routed experts shrink to k/E of their size in the bottom bar, which is the whole point of MoE: memory scales with the total, compute with the active part.

    Try: Llama 3.1 8B (the embedding and the separate output head are 13% of it), then SmolLM2 135M (tied embeddings: the one vocabulary matrix is 21% of a small model), then DeepSeek-V3 (the routed experts are almost everything in memory and a small sliver per token).

    The formulas, with this model's numbers

    Every count below is a product of config fields, written once in src/calc/calc.py and ported line for line to this page. Each block lists the formula, then the same formula with the chosen model's values, then the count for all layers of that kind. Weight matrices dominate; biases and norm gains are listed so the total is exact, not because they matter for cost.

    FLOPs: the 2N rule and the attention term
    Forward FLOPs per token = 2 × (every weight a token multiplies through, the LM head included, the input embedding lookup excluded) + the attention term. The attention term is, per attention layer, 2 × nh × (query-key dimension + value dimension) FLOPs for every cached position the token reads: one multiply-add per dimension for the score q·k, one per dimension for the weighted sum of values. It does not depend on nkv: grouped-query attention (GQA) shrinks the cache, not the attention FLOPs. Training costs about 3× the forward pass (backward is about twice forward), which gives the familiar 6N per token. This is the same counting as Kaplan et al. 2020 (Table 1: Cforward ≈ 2N + 2nlayernctxdattn, arXiv 2001.08361), whose context term is ours averaged over a causal prefill.

    Context length: where attention and the cache overtake the weights

    At short context a token's cost is its weights: 2 FLOPs per active parameter, and the whole weight set read once per decode step. Both attention costs grow linearly with the context: the FLOPs to score every cached position, and the bytes of the cache itself, multiplied by the batch. Somewhere they pass the weights. Where depends on the attention design, and that is what the variants on the Attention lab are for. Press play to sweep the same model from a short prompt to its longest context; switch the attention to see the same model as if it had been built with full multi-head attention (MHA, one key/value head per query head) or multi-query attention (MQA, one key/value head for all).

    Forward FLOPs per decoded token
    Memory for the batch: weights and cache (axis in decimal units, 1 GB = 109 bytes)
    What these curves leave out
    Decode FLOPs assume attention over the whole cache in the plain (non-tiled) form; FlashAttention changes the memory traffic, not the FLOPs. MLA is counted in the absorbed form for decode (each head scores the 576-wide cache directly: DeepSeek-V3's inference/model.py sets attn_impl = "absorb" by default at line 17 and computes the scores against kv_cache and pe_cache at lines 486 to 487, read 2026-10-18), which is why DeepSeek-V3's attention FLOPs per position are large while its cache is small. Sliding-window and chunked layers read at most their window. Recurrent layers (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet) are counted in their step-by-step form, with their fixed state taken as FP32. Weight bytes per step at batch 1 count only the experts one token uses; at larger batches, see the next section.

    Dense vs MoE at equal active parameters

    Take the chosen model and build its dense twin: every MoE layer replaced by one dense feed-forward block whose width is what a token actually uses (k routed experts plus the shared ones). The twin has the same active parameters and the same FLOPs per token. Step through what changes when the twin's feed-forward is cut into experts and more experts are added. For a dense model, the twin is the model itself and its MoE version splits each feed-forward block into 8 experts with 2 active (the Mixtral pattern).

    Compute it in your head

    Interview arithmetic. Each answer is computed live from the real config with the same code as the calculator, and shows the working. Rough mental numbers to carry: a 4096-wide layer's attention projections with 8 KV heads are about 42M parameters; a SwiGLU feed-forward block is 3df; BF16 is 2 bytes.

    Checked against the checkpoints

    The target is not the number in a model's name but the exact count of stored tensors that Hugging Face reports for each repository's safetensors files (read 2026-10-18 at the commit listed in src/calc/inputs/hf_param_counts.json). Those counts include things that are not the main model's parameters, so the check is: calculated main model + MTP layers + vision tower + anything else stored = Hub count, with every addition explained. The second check is the published headline: which way of counting rounds (or truncates) to the figure the vendor printed.

    Common mistakes

    Using the query head count for the KV cache
    The cache holds nkv heads, not nh. For Llama 3.1 8B that is 8, not 32: 128 KiB per token in BF16, not 512 KiB. Switch the attention to MHA in the context section to see the 4× difference on the same model.
    Assuming head_dim = hidden_size / num_heads
    Many configs set head_dim explicitly. Gemma 7B has 16 heads of 256 on a 3072-wide stream (16 × 256 = 4096 ≠ 3072); Qwen3 32B has 64 heads of 128 on a 5120-wide stream. hidden_size // num_attention_heads gives the wrong attention parameters and the wrong cache for both. Read head_dim when it is there.
    Counting the embedding twice when it is tied
    tie_word_embeddings: true means the output head reuses the input embedding matrix: count Vd once. It still costs 2Vd FLOPs per token as the head. And a tied checkpoint can still store both: Qwen3 0.6B's file saves lm_head.weight as its own tensor, which is why the Hub says 0.75B for a 0.6B model.
    Calling all MoE parameters "active", or the active count "the model size"
    A token uses k of E routed experts; all E must still be in memory. Mixtral 8x7B is not 56B (only the feed-forward blocks are replicated: attention, norms and embeddings are shared) and not 14B active (2 of 8 experts plus the shared parts is 12.9B). Vendors also differ on whether the active count includes the embedding and the head: the check table shows which convention reproduces each headline.
    Reading a quantised checkpoint's size as its parameter count
    The Hub's count of DeepSeek-V3 is 684.5B: 671.0B main model, 13.5B MTP layer, and 41.5M FP32 block-scale tensors that FP8 weights carry (one scale per 128 × 128 block). The same repository family is not consistent: the Hub counts the scale tensors for DeepSeek-V3 and V3.2-Exp but not for V3.2 or Kimi K2, although the files of all four contain them (checked in the shard headers).
    Forgetting that GQA does not cut attention FLOPs
    Sharing key/value heads shrinks the cache and the bytes read per step; every query head still scores every cached position. Long-context prefill is compute-bound on those scores whatever nkv is.
    Treating a sliding-window or chunked layer as global
    Gemma 3 27B keeps 5 of every 6 layers at a 1024-token window (512 on Gemma 3 1B); gpt-oss alternates 128-token windows with full attention; Mistral 7B v0.1 used a 4096 window everywhere. Their cache stops growing on those layers once the context passes the window, so a whole-model "KV per token × context" overstates them several times at long context.

    Interview questions

    Parameter count of a Llama-style model from its config?
    Vd (embedding) + Vd if untied (head) + L × [d(nh + 2nkv)dh + nhdhd (attention) + 3df (SwiGLU) + 2d (norms)] + d. For Llama 3.1 8B this is exactly 8,030,261,248, the stored count.
    FLOPs to train a 7B dense model on 2T tokens?
    About 6ND = 6 × 7e9 × 2e12 = 8.4e22, plus the attention term (small at 4k context for a 7B model, a few percent). Use the active N for an MoE.
    Why does decode at batch 1 run far below a GPU's peak FLOPs?
    Each step reads every active weight once (2 bytes per parameter in BF16) for 2 FLOPs per parameter: about 1 FLOP per byte. An H100 SXM needs about 295 FLOPs per byte (989.5 TFLOP/s dense BF16 over 3.35 TB/s, NVIDIA's figures) to be compute-bound, so batch-1 decode is memory-bound by two orders of magnitude. Batching reuses each weight read across sequences; the cache does not batch, since each sequence reads its own. See Performance math.
    Design: serve 128k-token contexts at batch 32 on one 80 GB GPU. What attention?
    Budget first: 32 × 131,072 = 4.2M cached tokens. After an 8B model's BF16 weights (16 GB), 64 GB is left: about 15 KB per cached token across all layers. Llama 3.1 8B's GQA cache is 128 KiB per token, 8.6× too much (550 GB for the batch); an FP8 cache halves that and still misses. DeepSeek-V3's MLA is 576 numbers per layer, but over 61 layers that is 69 KiB per token: it misses too. A hybrid with only a few attention layers fits: Nemotron-H 8B (4 attention layers out of 52) needs 16 KiB per token plus 99 MiB of recurrent state per sequence, 72 GB for the batch in BF16 (over) and 38 GB with an FP8 cache (fits beside the weights). So: few attention layers or windows on most of them, few KV heads, an FP8 cache, and then check quality on long-context evaluations, since that is what these savings cost. Every number here is from the calculator above.
    Why did DeepSeek choose MLA, and what does it cost?
    It caches one 512-wide latent plus a 64-wide shared RoPE key per layer (576 numbers) instead of 2 × 128 heads × 128: a cache per token about 57× smaller than MHA at the same head count. The cost is compute: decode scores every position against the 576-wide latent in every head, so attention FLOPs per position are larger than MHA's, and RoPE has to be split off into a decoupled key. See the MLA explainer.
    Dense 8B or MoE 30B-A3B for the same serving budget?
    The MoE costs fewer FLOPs per token (3.3B active) but needs memory for 30.5B parameters, and at large batches its decode steps read most experts, so its bytes per step approach the full model's. It wins when memory is plentiful and compute or latency at small batch is the limit; the dense model wins on a memory-limited device.

    The code

    The formulas live once, in src/calc/calc.py (standard library only); parts/33_js_cc_1core.js is a line-by-line port. Below: the parameter functions as they ran, the validation output, and the check that the page's JavaScript gives the same numbers as the Python on every config at five context lengths.

    calc.py: mixer_params, ffn_params and params (from line 236)
    def mixer_params(m, d): """Parameters of one sequence mixer, split into (matmul weights, other: biases, norms, small vectors).""" if m is None: return 0, 0 t = m['t'] if t == 'attn': q = d * m['nh'] * m['hd'] * (2 if m['gate'] else 1) kv = 2 * d * m['nkv'] * m['hd'] o = m['nh'] * m['hdv'] * d oth = (m['nh'] * m['hd'] * (2 if m['gate'] else 1) + 2 * m['nkv'] * m['hd'] if m['bqkv'] else 0) + \ (d if m['bo'] else 0) + m['qk'] + (m['nh'] if m['sinks'] else 0) return q + kv + o, oth if t == 'mla': nh = m['nh']; qh = m['nope'] + m['rope'] if m['ql']: q = d * m['ql'] + m['ql'] * nh * qh; oth = m['ql'] else: q = d * nh * qh; oth = 0 kv = d * (m['kvl'] + m['rope']) + m['kvl'] * nh * (m['nope'] + m['v']) oth += m['kvl'] o = nh * m['v'] * d mm = q + kv + o if m['inh']: mm += (m['ql'] or d) * m['inh'] * m['ihd'] + d * m['ihd'] + d * m['inh'] oth += 2 * m['ihd'] return mm, oth if t == 'mamba2': di = m['nh'] * m['hd']; gs = 2 * m['ng'] * m['ds'] inp = d * (2 * di + gs + m['nh']); out = di * d conv_dim = di + gs oth = conv_dim * m['k'] + (conv_dim if m['cb'] else 0) + 3 * m['nh'] + (di if m['norm'] else 0) if m['pb']: oth += 2 * di + gs + m['nh'] + d return inp + out, oth if t == 'mamba1': di = m['di']; ds = m['ds']; r = m['dtr'] mm = d * 2 * di + di * (r + 2 * ds) + r * di + di * d oth = di * m['k'] + (di if m['cb'] else 0) + di + di * ds + di if m['pb']: oth += 2 * di + d if m['xn']: oth += r + 2 * ds # Jamba's dt, B and C RMSNorms return mm, oth if t == 'gdn': kd = m['nk'] * m['dk']; vd = m['nv'] * m['dv'] mm = d * (2 * kd + 2 * vd) + d * 2 * m['nv'] + vd * d oth = (2 * kd + vd) * m['k'] + 2 * m['nv'] + m['dv'] return mm, oth raise ValueError(t) def ffn_params(f, d): """Returns dict: dense matmul, dense other, routed experts (all), shared, router (matmul), other.""" r = {'dense': 0, 'dense_o': 0, 'routed': 0, 'routed_o': 0, 'shared': 0, 'router': 0, 'moe_o': 0} if f is None: return r if f['t'] == 'glu': r['dense'] = 3 * d * f['ff']; r['dense_o'] = (2 * f['ff'] + d) if f['bias'] else 0 elif f['t'] == 'mlp': r['dense'] = 2 * d * f['ff']; r['dense_o'] = (f['ff'] + d) if f['bias'] else 0 else: E = f['E'] r['routed'] = E * 3 * d * f['ff'] r['routed_o'] = E * (2 * f['ff'] + d) if f['ebias'] else 0 r['shared'] = 3 * d * f['sff'] + (d if f['sgate'] else 0) r['router'] = d * E r['moe_o'] = (E if f['rbias'] else 0) + (E if f['cbias'] else 0) return r def params(spec): d = spec['d']; V = spec['V'] b = {'embedding': V * d + spec.get('pos_embed', 0), 'unembedding': 0 if spec['tied'] else V * d, 'attention': 0, 'ssm': 0, 'ffn_dense': 0, 'moe_routed': 0, 'moe_shared': 0, 'router': 0, 'norms': spec.get('final_norm', d) * (2 if spec.get('norm_bias') else 1), 'biases_other': 0} act = {'routed': 0}; mm = 0 # matmul weights a token touches for lay in spec['layers']: b['norms'] += lay['norms'] for key in ('mix', 'mix2'): m = lay.get(key) if m is None: continue w, o = mixer_params(m, d) if m['t'] in ('attn', 'mla'): b['attention'] += w + o else: b['ssm'] += w + o mm += w f = ffn_params(lay['ffn'], d) b['ffn_dense'] += f['dense'] + f['dense_o'] b['moe_routed'] += f['routed'] + f['routed_o'] b['moe_shared'] += f['shared'] b['router'] += f['router'] + f['moe_o'] mm += f['dense'] + f['shared'] + f['router'] if lay['ffn'] and lay['ffn']['t'] == 'moe': per = (f['routed'] + f['routed_o']) / lay['ffn']['E'] act['routed'] += per * lay['ffn']['k'] mm += 3 * d * lay['ffn']['ff'] * lay['ffn']['k'] total = sum(b.values()) active = total - b['moe_routed'] + act['routed'] mm += V * d # LM head matmul (also when tied) mtp = 0 if spec.get('mtp'): # one extra decoder layer like the last layer, plus a 2d x d projection and three norms (DeepSeek: eh_proj, # enorm, hnorm, shared_head.norm; Qwen3-Next: fc, two pre-fc norms, norm); DeepSeek and GLM also store a copy # of the embedding and the head inside the MTP layer last = spec['layers'][-1] w, o = mixer_params(last['mix'], d); f = ffn_params(last['ffn'], d) one = w + o + sum(f.values()) + last['norms'] + 2 * d * d + 3 * d mtp = spec['mtp'] * (one + (2 * V * d if spec.get('mtp_copy') else 0)) active = int(round(active)) return {'breakdown': b, 'total': int(total), 'active': active, 'active_no_emb': active - b['embedding'], 'active_no_emb_head': active - b['embedding'] - b['unembedding'], 'matmul_active': int(round(mm)), 'mtp': int(mtp)}

    The other tabs build a transformer from its parts. This one opens trained models and measures what they do with those parts: which earlier tokens each attention head reads, where attention goes when nothing is worth reading, how large the residual stream grows, and what the model would predict if it stopped after layer k. Each measurement explains a design decision met elsewhere on this page.

    In one screen

    The models. SmolLM2-135M (Hugging Face, Apache-2.0, revision 93efa2f): a Llama-architecture model with 30 layers, 9 query heads sharing 3 key-value heads, width 576, RoPE, RMSNorm before each sub-layer, tied input and output embeddings. Qwen3-0.6B (Alibaba, Apache-2.0, revision c1899de, run in float16): 28 layers, 16 query heads on 8 key-value heads, width 1,024, plus RMSNorm on every query and key (QK-norm). Pythia-70M-deduped (EleutherAI, Apache-2.0): 6 layers of 8 heads, with checkpoints published from the start of training, which we read but did not train. And the tiny GPT of this topic (6 layers, 8 heads, width 256, trained here on TinyStories; see the running example). The text is the running sequence, the story of Roxy the rhinoceros, re-tokenised by each model's own tokenizer.

    Terms. An attention weight aij is how much query position i reads from key position j: one row of the softmax over the scores qi·kj/√d, so each row sums to 1. A head is one such pattern; a layer has several. The residual stream is the vector each token carries from layer to layer; every attention and feed-forward sub-layer reads it and adds its output back.

    All values measured on an Apple M1 Pro (MPS for SmolLM2 and Qwen3, CPU for Pythia and the tiny GPT), 2026-10-18, torch 2.14.1, transformers 5.20.1. These are deterministic forward passes on fixed inputs: what transfers to a datacenter GPU is everything here except the timings (none are quoted).

    Where the attention weights come from

    The problem. Fast attention kernels never build the T × T matrix of weights: FlashAttention and PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention (SDPA) stream over keys and keep only running sums (FlashAttention). So the weights you want to look at do not exist in a normal forward pass.

    How to get them. Load the model with attn_implementation="eager". Eager attention is the textbook arithmetic, and it returns the weights. In transformers v5.20.1 (commit 0ea8779), src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py, which SmolLM2 runs:

    180 def eager_attention_forward(module, query, key, value, attention_mask, scaling, dropout=0.0, **kwargs): 190 key_states = repeat_kv(key, module.num_key_value_groups) # GQA: copy each KV head to its query heads 191 value_states = repeat_kv(value, module.num_key_value_groups) 193 attn_weights = torch.matmul(query, key_states.transpose(2, 3)) * scaling # (B, H, T, T) scores 195 attn_weights = attn_weights + attention_mask # causal mask: -inf above the diagonal 197 attn_weights = nn.functional.softmax(attn_weights, dim=-1, dtype=torch.float32).to(query.dtype) 199 attn_output = torch.matmul(attn_weights, value_states) 202 return attn_output, attn_weights

    Lines 180 to 202, abridged (signature joined, comments ours). Lines 253 to 255 pick the function: ALL_ATTENTION_FUNCTIONS.get_interface(self.config._attn_implementation, eager_attention_forward); line 331 records each LlamaAttention's second output as outputs.attentions. The softmax runs in float32 even for a float16 model (line 197). Qwen3 differs only by RMSNorm on queries and keys first (modeling_qwen3.py lines 229 and 244). Lines located by pattern: src/inside/locate_source.py.

    The mistake. With the default SDPA path, asking for weights gives nothing usable. Our run printed:

    From src/inside/extract_pretrained.py (SDPA's function returns attn_output, None: integrations/sdpa_attention.py line 182). The cost of eager: it materialises B·H·T² weights per layer, which is fine for 226 tokens and out of the question at 128k.

    How we measure the rest without editing the library: transformers lets you register your own attention function (AttentionInterface.register). Ours is the eager arithmetic plus a rule about which keys a query may see; with no rule it reproduces the model's loss exactly ( on the running text, both ways). The sink and window experiments below only change that rule.

    Go deeper. The arithmetic of one attention layer, with shapes and FLOPs: Block lab. What each head must cache: Attention lab.

    Attention maps: what each head reads

    The problem. "Attention lets every token look at every earlier token" says what a head may do. A trained model uses that freedom very unevenly, and the patterns it settles on are what the architecture choices on this page are really about: a head that only ever reads the previous token needs no long cache; a head that parks most of its weight on token 0 is why streaming caches keep that token.

    How to read the explorer. The grid has one cell per head of SmolLM2-135M (rows are layers 0 to 29, columns heads 0 to 8), coloured by the score you pick. Click a cell to draw that head's map: row i is query token i, column j key token j, darker means more weight, and everything above the diagonal is empty because of the causal mask. Click a token in the text to see what it reads in that head.

    Colour heads by

    What the explorer shows (scores defined under the grid, all on the running text unless noted):

    • Previous-token heads put most of their weight on token i−1. They exist from layer 1 on in SmolLM2; the strongest is (score ). They are the first half of an induction circuit (next section): they copy "what came before me" into each token's residual stream, so a later head can search for it.
    • First-token heads appear abruptly at layer 12: below it, the mean weight on token 0 is at most in every layer; from layer 12 on it is to per layer (mean over the 9 heads, queries from position 8). That is the attention sink (section 4).
    • Spread is the head's entropy divided by the most it could be (log of the number of visible keys): 1 means uniform reading, near 0 means one key. Layer 0 heads are the broadest; they average over the recent context.

    When it matters. Head patterns decide what can be pruned, cached or windowed. Gemma 3 and gpt-oss make most layers local (a sliding window) because most heads read nearby tokens; they keep some global layers for the few heads that do not (Architecture map). How to check it on any model: eager attention, a few hundred tokens, and the three scores above: about 20 lines (head_scores in src/inside/make_page_data.py).

    Induction heads: how a transformer copies from its context

    The problem. Much of what a language model does with its context is copying: a name introduced in sentence one, a variable defined at the top of a file, a phrase the user typed. The model cannot store those in its weights; it must find them in the context at run time. Olsson et al. (Anthropic, 2022, In-context learning and induction heads) traced much of this to one circuit, the induction head, and reported "a phase change that occurs early in training for language models of every size" when it appears.

    How it works. Two heads in two layers. A previous-token head (section 2) writes into each position j the identity of token j−1. Later, at the current position whose token is A, an induction head builds a query that means "find positions whose previous token was A". It matches the position right after the earlier A, reads its token B, and raises B's logit. The rule it implements: [A][B] ... [A] → predict [B]. It needs two layers because the "previous token" information must already sit in the key before the second head can match on it.

    The clean test. Feed a block of random tokens twice: <|endoftext|> R R, with R = 100 token ids drawn uniformly (8 random draws, seed 0). On the first copy nothing can be predicted, so the loss is near or above log(vocabulary). On the second copy every token is predictable by copying. The induction score of a head is its mean attention weight, over queries in the second copy, on the token just after the earlier occurrence of the current token: the exact place an induction head should look.

    Before and after training: the same repeated sequence through Pythia-70M

    One input, published checkpoints of one training run. Top: loss on each position of the sequence (first copy left of the line, second copy right). Bottom: what the strongest induction head of that checkpoint reads from one query in the second copy (position 150), with the "right place to look" marked. published checkpoints measured here (CPU)

    The phase change: induction score against tokens trained

    Unexpected, and kept: Pythia-70M forgets how to copy random tokens late in training
    On the random sequence, copying is best at step (B tokens; second-copy loss ) and then erodes: at the final step 143,000 the second-copy loss is back to , although a head still puts of its weight on the right token and the loss on the running text barely moves ( to ). So the head still finds the token, but the circuit no longer raises its logit for out-of-distribution ids, and the first-copy loss climbs too (: ever more confident, wrong guesses). Why is unconfirmed; we did not investigate. The lesson for testing: repeated random tokens test the mechanism on inputs unlike training data, so read them together with a natural-text copy test. Step through the late checkpoints in the animation above.

    The tiny GPT does not get there. Trained here for 1,500 steps (12.3M tokens, about 5 minutes), it never forms an induction head: its best induction score is and its loss on the second copy of random tokens () is no better than on the first (; both above log 4,096 = 8.32, because random ids are far outside TinyStories). Even a repeated 127-token passage of real validation text only drops from to . That is a budget fact, not an architecture fact: Pythia-70M, the same shape (6 layers of 8 heads), formed its induction head between and billion tokens (chart above), about times our whole run. What the tiny GPT does learn is to reuse the name it has just read. The four tokens of "Roxy" are R, o, x, y; predicting x after R o needs the context. Its loss on each of the 11 xs in the running sequence:

    So the tiny GPT reuses a name from its context although no classic induction head shows (its best induction score on repeated random tokens is ): how it does so is unconfirmed (not investigated here). The transformer from zero tracks the same reuse through training: on the same retrain, the three tokens after R cost 9.0 nats together at the name’s first appearance, 4.5 at the second and 1.6 on average from the third on, and the drop for repeats starts at step 500.

    The cost and when it matters. An induction head needs the earlier tokens kept in full: that is the case for attention with a KV cache and against a fixed-size state. Jelassi et al. (2024, Repeat After Me) show that transformers "dramatically outperform state space models at copying and retrieving information from context"; hybrids keep a few attention layers largely for this (Reading: beyond attention). Sliding-window layers can only copy within their window. How to check a model or a change: the repeated-random-tokens loss (first copy against second copy) is a 10-line test that needs no labels; run it after any change to attention, position encoding or caching.

    Attention sinks: where attention goes when nothing is worth reading

    The problem. Softmax weights must sum to 1. A head that has nothing useful to read at some position still has to put its weight somewhere. Trained models settle on one place: the first token. Xiao et al. (2023, StreamingLLM) named this the attention sink. The first token is a natural dump: every later query can see it, and its residual vector can be made distinctive (section 5) so that a head can match it without moving the output much.

    Weight on the first token, by layer

    The first token, whatever it is. Neither SmolLM2's nor Qwen3's tokenizer adds a beginning-of-sequence token by default, so above the sink sits on the word "Once". Put <|endoftext|> in front and the sink moves to it: in SmolLM2, the weight left on "Once" falls to at most per layer, and the loss on the same text tokens moves from to .

    What happens when the sink is removed. Our attention function can forbid every query from reading token 0 (each row renormalises over the other keys). Same model, same text:

    The greedy continuation of "Once upon a time," shows what that loss means (SmolLM2, 40 new tokens, real outputs):

    Before and after: a sliding window with and without the sink, on the same long text

    1,024 tokens of TinyStories validation stories through SmolLM2. Each query may read only the last 64 tokens (a sliding-window cache), or those 64 plus the first 4 tokens (StreamingLLM's fix). Positions stay as they are; with RoPE, masking keys is the same as evicting them from a cache. Step through the query positions; the strip shows which keys the query can read under each rule, and the chart the loss per block of 32 tokens. measured here (MPS)

    StreamingLLM's abstract states that window attention "fails when the text length surpasses the cache size" and that "keeping the KV of initial tokens will largely recover the performance". Our small run reproduces both, independently; here a single kept token recovers as much as four ( against , Qwen3: against ).

    Designs that build the sink in. Instead of letting a model hijack a real token, give every head somewhere to put weight on purpose. In gpt-oss, "each attention head has a learned bias in the denominator of the softmax", which lets a head "pay no attention to any tokens" (OpenAI, gpt-oss model card, section 2.2, 2025-08-08; the tiny GPT's sink preset implements it, Attention lab). StreamingLLM also trained models with a dedicated learnable sink token. When it matters: any cache that evicts tokens (sliding windows, streaming chat, KV compression) must keep the sink, and any quantisation or pruning scheme must leave the first token's enormous vector alone (next section). How to check: the mean weight on token 0 by layer, as in the chart, takes one eager forward pass.

    Massive activations and the growing residual stream

    The problem. In a pre-norm block (the norm sits before each sub-layer, Block lab), every sub-layer adds its output to the residual stream and nothing ever rescales it. So the stream's size is free to grow with depth, and a model can use that freedom to make a few numbers enormous. Sun et al. (2024, Massive Activations in Large Language Models) found such "massive activations" across many LLMs, sometimes about 100,000 times the typical value (paraphrase of their abstract); they sit in a few fixed dimensions on a few tokens (often the first), stay nearly constant whatever the input, act like bias terms, and are what lets attention concentrate on those tokens. That is the mechanism behind the sinks of the previous section.

    Size of the residual stream after each layer

    What we measured. In SmolLM2, one dimension of the residual stream (dimension of 576) on the first token reaches at layer 12 and stays above until the last block, while the median absolute value of an entry at that depth is about : a ratio of about to 1. Layer 12 is exactly where the sink switched on (section 4). In layers 3 to 9 the same dimension already reaches about , on token 4, the first comma ("Once upon a time,"), while the weight on token 0 in those layers is still small (0.07 to 0.09): the big value moves to the first token at the layer where the sink appears. The tiny GPT, which never formed a sink, also has no massive activation: its largest entry after training is . Qwen3-0.6B:

    Why an architect cares.

    • Quantisation. A single entry of 20,000 next to entries of about 1 wrecks a per-tensor int8 scale: Dettmers et al. (LLM.int8(), 2022) keep such outlier dimensions in 16 bits. See Quantization and Precision.
    • Number formats. float16 tops out at 65,504; a stream that grows to tens of thousands is close. bfloat16 has the range (and less precision), which is one reason training moved to it (Numerical computing).
    • The final norm. Because the stream's scale drifts with depth, pre-norm models need a norm before the unembedding (self.norm at modeling_llama.py line 402). Post-norm models renormalise after every block instead and pay for it in stability (Block lab).
    • Designs. Learned sinks (gpt-oss) and QK-norm (Qwen3, OLMo 2, Gemma 3) give heads other ways to say "nothing here", which may reduce the pressure to grow such values (unconfirmed for these models); Sun et al. trained GPT-2 with explicit attention biases and report that "massive activations disappear" (section 4.3; not run here).

    How to check: hook the output of every decoder layer (a forward hook, as in extract_pretrained.py; the hidden_states output of a Hugging Face model applies the final norm to its last entry) and print the largest |x| per layer with its token and dimension.

    The logit lens: what would the model say if it stopped here?

    The idea (nostalgebraist, 2020, interpreting GPT: the logit lens). The residual stream is one shared space that every layer writes into and the unembedding finally reads. So apply the model's own final norm and unembedding to the stream after layer k and read off a next-token distribution. If the stream is a gradually refined prediction, the early guesses should drift towards the final one.

    SmolLM2's guess at every layer, token by token

    Rows are layers (0 = the embedding, 30 = the model's output); columns are positions in the running text. Each cell shows the top-1 predicted next token at that layer; green means the true next token got high probability. Drag to move through the text. measured here (MPS)

    How good is each layer's guess?

    What we measured.

    When it matters and the caveat. The lens is a cheap first look at where in depth a prediction forms, useful when deciding where to cut layers (early exit, layer pruning) or where to read features from. It is not exact: middle layers may encode the answer in directions the final unembedding does not read, which is why the tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023, arXiv 2303.08112) learns a small map per layer (not run here). How to check: model.lm_head(model.model.norm(h)) for each hooked h; the last layer must reproduce the model's logits exactly (ours: max difference ).

    Common mistakes, drills and interview questions

    Mistakes we made or saw on this tab

    Asking for attention weights with SDPA or FlashAttention
    transformers prints a warning and outputs.attentions is not a usable list of tensors (section 1). Load with attn_implementation="eager", or switch with model.set_attn_implementation("eager"), and keep the sequence short: eager attention materialises every weight.
    Reading the last hidden_states entry as the raw residual stream
    In Hugging Face models the last entry comes after the final norm, so its size is not comparable to the others, and applying the norm again in a logit lens normalises twice. Hook the decoder layers instead (section 5).
    Expecting induction heads in a small, briefly trained model
    We did: the tiny GPT trained here for 12.3M tokens has none (section 3). Whether a mechanism exists is a question of training tokens as much as of architecture; Pythia-70M, same shape, needed far more. When an ablation of a tiny model "shows" that an architecture cannot copy, check the budget first.
    Evicting the first tokens from a sliding cache
    The loss on SmolLM2 roughly doubles once the window slides past the start (section 4). Keep the sink tokens, or train with a sink.
    Calling every head with high weight on token 0 "broken"
    The sink is a learned no-op, not a fault. Forbidding it raised the loss and broke generation (section 4).
    Quantising activations with one scale per tensor
    One entry of about 20,000 (section 5) forces a scale that rounds every ordinary entry to zero in int8. Use per-token or per-channel scales, or keep outlier channels in 16 bits.

    Predict, then reveal

    Interview questions

    What is an attention sink, and why does it form?
    Softmax weights sum to 1, so a head with nothing to read must still put its weight somewhere; models learn to dump it on the first token, which every query can see and whose vector they make distinctive (massive activations). In SmolLM2 the mean weight on token 0 jumps above 0.3 from layer 12, in the same layer where one dimension of the first token's residual reaches about 20,000.
    Why does a sliding-window KV cache fail, and what is the fix?
    Once the first tokens leave the window, the heads lose their sink and spread weight over tokens they would have ignored. Keep the first few tokens' keys and values (StreamingLLM), or train with a learned sink (gpt-oss). Measured here: 1.62 full, 3.36 window only, 1.81 window plus sink (mean loss after the first 64 tokens).
    What is an induction head, and why does it need two layers?
    [A][B] ... [A] → [B]. A previous-token head first writes "my predecessor was A" into position B's residual; a later head's query (current token A) matches that key and copies B. The second head can only match on information a first head has already moved, hence two layers.
    Design: you replace 3 of every 4 attention layers with SSM layers. What do you test first, and why?
    Copying and retrieval from context, because that is what a fixed-size state cannot do and induction heads do: the repeated-random-tokens loss (first copy against second), a needle or name-recall test at the target length, and the loss on long documents by position. Check which attention layers held the induction heads in the original model, and keep attention where they were; keep the sink behaviour if the remaining attention layers use windows.
    Your int8 model's quality collapses but the weights quantise fine. Where do you look?
    The activations: a few dimensions on a few tokens (often the first) are thousands of times larger than the rest. Print max |x| per layer with its token and dimension; use per-token or per-channel scales or mixed precision for the outlier channels.
    What does the logit lens tell you, and when does it mislead?
    Where in depth the next-token prediction forms, using the model's own unembedding on intermediate states. It misleads where intermediate layers use directions the unembedding ignores (SmolLM2's middle layers give worse than uniform guesses although the model is fine); the tuned lens corrects that with a learned map per layer.

    Scripts and recorded outputs: src/inside/ (extract_pretrained.py, pythia_phase.py, train_snapshots.py, tiny_analysis.py, make_page_data.py; outputs in src/inside/out/). Models: SmolLM2-135M revision 93efa2f097d58c2a74874c7e644dbc9b0cee75a2; Qwen3-0.6B revision c1899de289a04d12100db370d81485cdf75e47ca; Pythia-70M-deduped revisions listed in src/inside/out/pythia_manifest.json.

    Common mistakes when reading a config

    Applying the GQA formula to an MLA model
    DeepSeek-V3's config.json says num_key_value_heads: 128. Plugging that into 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x 2 bytes gives 3,904 KiB per token (with 128-dimension values), about 3.8 MiB. MLA caches one latent of kv_lora_rank (512) plus one RoPE key of qk_rope_head_dim (64) per layer: 576 x 61 x 2 bytes = 68.6 KiB. The field is there for the code path that rebuilds heads; check for kv_lora_rank before using it.
    Counting sliding-window layers at full cost
    Gemma 3 27B stores 496 KiB per token if every layer is counted, which is 62 GiB for one 131,072-token sequence. 52 of its 62 layers keep only the last 1,024 tokens, so the real figure is 10.4 GiB. The per-token number is still right for the first 1,024 tokens; past the window the windowed layers stop growing.
    Reading max_position_embeddings as the trained context
    MiniMax-M1's config says 10,240,000 while its model card says it natively supports 1 million tokens. Qwen3 32B's config says 40,960 while the card says 32,768 natively and 131,072 with YaRN. The config field is the size the code allows; the trained and evaluated length is in the card or paper, and going past it needs the scaling the card names.
    Reading a per-head key count off the wrong layers
    Gemma 4 31B lists num_key_value_heads: 16 with head_dim: 256, but those apply to the 50 sliding layers. Its 10 global layers use num_global_key_value_heads: 4 of global_head_dim: 512 and store one tensor for both K and V (attention_k_eq_v). Counting all 60 layers the sliding way gives 960 KiB per token; the config's own layer types give 840 KiB.
    Treating active parameters as the memory you need
    gpt-oss-120b runs 5.1B parameters per token, but all 117B must sit in memory (the model card's point is that it fits one 80 GB GPU in its MXFP4 format). "17B" in Llama 4 Maverick's name is the active count; the total is 400B. Mixtral 8x7B is 46.7B in total, not 56B, because only the FFN is replicated eight times.

    Notes on the data

    • Sources. Shapes come from each model's config.json on Hugging Face (copies in src/map/inputs/configs/, fetched 2026-10-18; gated Meta and Google repos read from public mirrors with the same shapes). GPT-3 and PaLM have no public config: their rows use the papers' tables. Dates, licences and parameter counts link to the model card, paper or announcement in each row's card; where a 2025 or 2026 date comes only from Sebastian Raschka's LLM Architecture Gallery (a third-party list, Apache 2.0) the row says "gallery".
    • Calculations. Every KV figure is derived: bf16, 2 bytes per number; full cost counts every cache-growing layer; "at 128K" credits windows. The figures agree with the gallery page's independent recalculation for every model the two share. DeepSeek-V4-Pro's compressed caches are not computed here.
    • Labels from configs. Attention, window and mixer labels are read from config fields; norm placement, QK-norm and activation come from the paper or card cited in the row (the configs rarely state them).
    • Not covered here. Closed frontier models (no configs), encoder and encoder-decoder families (the Families and objectives page), tokenizer details (Tokenizers), benchmark quality and prices (Topic: llm-landscape).

    Best outside resources

    Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled outthird-party

    Andrej Karpathy, January 2023. A decoder written live in PyTorch, from bigrams to self-attention, residuals and LayerNorm. Pairs with nanoGPT and the newer nanochat. about 2 h

    The Annotated Transformerthird-party

    Harvard NLP (2018, updated 2022): the original paper interleaved with runnable code, encoder-decoder and all. about 1 h 30 min

    The Illustrated Transformerthird-party

    Jay Alammar, 2018. Pictures of Q, K, V and multi-head attention; the gentlest first read. about 30 min

    How to Scale Your Model: All the Transformer Mathmaker

    Google DeepMind authors, 2025. Parameters, FLOPs and KV cache per component, worked; the best companion to section 8. about 1 h

    Transformer Inference Arithmeticthird-party

    kipply, 2022. KV cache, memory-bound decode and FLOP counting for serving. about 40 min

    Transformer Math 101third-party

    EleutherAI, April 2023. The 6N rule, memory for training, worked numbers. about 25 min

    The Big LLM Architecture Comparisonthird-party

    Sebastian Raschka, from July 2025, kept updated, with the LLM Architecture Gallery: what changed inside the block from DeepSeek-V3 onward, with diagrams. about 1 h

    The Transformer Family, Version 2.0third-party

    Lilian Weng, January 2023. A survey of attention, position and efficiency variants up to 2022; a map of names. about 1 h 30 min

    A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuitsmaker

    Anthropic, December 2021. The residual stream as a communication channel, heads as independent read-write operations; with In-context learning and induction heads (2022). about 2 h for both

    interpreting GPT: the logit lensthird-party

    nostalgebraist, 2020. Decode the residual stream after every layer. about 20 min

    Rotary Embeddings: A Relative Revolutionthird-party

    EleutherAI, 2021. RoPE derived and compared, from the team that first trained it at scale. about 25 min

    A Visual Guide to Mixture of Expertsthird-party

    Maarten Grootendorst, 2024. Routers, top-k, capacity and balancing in pictures; his visual guide to Mamba does the same for SSMs. about 40 min each

    State Space Duality (Mamba-2)maker

    Tri Dao, May 2024, four parts. How SSMs and linear attention are the same computation, by Mamba's co-author. about 1 h

    Stanford CS336: Language Modeling from Scratchthird-party

    Course with lectures on architectures, hyperparameters and MoE, and assignments that build and train a transformer. a course: tens of hours; the architecture lecture about 1 h 20 min
